Before proceeding with the Orders of the Day, I desire, as I announced yesterday, to engage the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine, indeed the right hon. the leader of the government and his associates in the cabinet, to a report appearing in the Montreal ' Daily Star ' of the 17th instant, by Ship-master John Taylor, of Nova Scotia, headed :

British Consul declares Canada has no flag.
I might here state, Mr. Speaker, that I intend concluding with a motion. The report reads as follows :

Threatened to fine Capt. Taylor £100 if he continued to use Canadian emblem.
Captain John Taylor, of the three-masted schooner ' M. J. Taylor,' is in this port at present. Captain Taylor has a grievance.
Captain Taylor hails from Nova Scotia. His ship is registered in Parrsboro, N.S., and has always flown what he considered the Canadian flag, the red ensign of the British merchant service, with the Canadian coat-of-arms in the lower right hand corner. - Captain Taylor related the reason for his grievance to the ' Star ' this morning, as follows :-
' I had been sailing around the different ports of South America all winter, and last January I sailed in the port of Rio Grande do Sul, in the Argentine republic, with cargo. We lay there for some time, and as there were a number of vessels in the harbour whose masters were friends of mine, our flag, the Canadian ensign, was flying at our peak most of the time.
' Some three or four days after its first appearance, I received a verbal warning from the British consul, Mr. Ray Stamford, that I was not flying the right flag. He ordered me to haul down that flag and run up the ' Red Ensign.' Well, I have knocked around pretty well, and in the last few years have been in a good many corners of the globe, and the Canadian flag was always good enough for other British consuls, so I thought it would do for Mr. Ray Stamford. I therefore took no notice of his warning.
' Then I did get it. I received a notice stating that I was liable to a fine of £100 if I continued to fly that flag. The notice bore the stamp of the consulate, and ordered me to appear at the consulate with my flag the following day.
' Well, you know the British consul is a man's only friend down there if he gets into trouble ; and I thought it better not to disobey. So I took the flag to him. He ordered me to cut out the Canadian coat-of-arms and fill the space with red bunting. I 'refused, and he had it done himself.
'This I consider quite unjustifiable. We Canadians were given the right to fly our flag in 1867. I have carried that flag at the mast head when lying in the midst of the British Mediterranean squadron at the Malta dock yards, at Cadiz, at Havre, and most of the Mediterranean British North and South Ameri-

can ports, and there has never been any exception taken to it until now.'
Captain Taylor is addressing a letter to the Board ot Trade about this matter, and desires to know if the action of the consul was justifiable. He says that he is a loyal Britisher, but is also a loyal Canadian : and he wants the right to fly what he maintains is the Canadian ensign.
I might here state that although this, to my mind, is an outrageous act on the part of the British consul, and wholly unauthorized and unprovoked, it is not the first time I had occasion to bring a subject of complaint of this nature to the notice of the government by way of seeking redress. It will be remembered by reference to ' Hansard ' that on the 3rd day of May, 1901, I brought to the notice of the government the case of the ship ' Canada,' belonging to the port of Lunenburg, N.S., Captain Arch. Conrod, master, which was floating the Canadian ensign of which, I am pleased to say, we, as Canadians have cause to be proud, in the port of Bahia, Brazil, on the 1st of March, 1901, when the British consul boarded the ship, and peremptorily required of the master to haul his flag down, informing him that it was a gross violation, or infringement of rights, and failing to do so, he would impose a fine of £500 and hold the ship for the penalty until paid. The captain rather than find himself and owners in trouble complied with the request. Peeling naturally much exercised over an apparent insult of this sort. I made special request of the government at the time, that inquiry be made of the British government, as to whether the master of the ' Canada ' was within his rights in floating the Canadian ensign in a foreign port, and if found that the captain was in error, then to arrange with the British Admiralty for authority, and thereby have the Canadian flag treated with the respect Canada is entitled to receive. However, subsequently having ascertained Canada was within her rights in floating her Canadian ensign, having obtained the authority from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty under power invested in them by the Imperial Merchants' Shipping (colours) Act of 1889, 1 inquired as to whether the authority had been officially communicated to the authorities in Canada, and found that it had. The royal warrant having issued under seal dated London, February 2, 1892, by the commissioners for executing the office of Lord High Admiralty of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, reads as follows :
Whereas we deem it expedient that Canadian registered vessels shall be permitted to wear the red ensign of Hts Majesty's fleet, with a Canadian coat-of-arms on the fly thereof.
We do therefore, by virtue of the power, and authority vested in us, hereby warrant, and authorize the red ensign of His Majesty's
fleet, with the Canadian coat-of-arms in the fly to be used on board vessels registered in the Dominion.
Given under our hands, and the seal of the Office of the Admiralty this 2nd day of February, 1892.
(Signed) H. FAIRFAX.

By command of their Lordships.
(Signed) Evan MacGregor.
To this a circular letter was issued by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa, which reads as follows
In accordance with the permission granted by the above warrant, the following regulations have been adopted by the Canadian government :-
1.	The area of the shield shall in no case exceed one-fourth the area of the Union Jack of the particular ensign.
2.	The shield shall be placed centrally in that part of the fly which is beyond the Jack.
(Signed) WILLIAM SMITH, Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Department of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa, June 10, 1895.
I desire to state here, that my object in bringing this subject of the Canadian flag prominently before parliament at present, is to have the world understand that Canada has a flag, composed of the British ensign with the Canadian coat of arms in the red fly thereof, and has authority to fly it. My object also is to urge the government of Canada to commuflicAe with the office of the Lord High Admiralty in London, through the Secretary of State for the colonies, asking that all British consuls throughout the world be advised of Canada's position as respects her flag, particularly the consuls of Bahia and Rio-Grande-do-suI Brazil, in order that the unnatural and outrageous treatment extended to Canadian shipmasters, sailing Canadian ships, when visiting the various ports, particularly those referred to, cannot ignore the Canadian flag in future, and that all Canadian shipmasters, and the merchant marine of Canada may be advised as well, by a public notice issued by the Department of Marine of Canada and published in the Canadian ' Gazette, ' informing the public of Canada's right to float her Canadian ensign in every sea.
It is wonderful the great instinct of the human race, the great delight we possess in the flying of flags. There is a something innate in man causing him to be enthused by a significant emblem raised in the air, whether it has the insignia of office or descent, or as the symbol of race or nationality -our national flag-it matters not. The flag of old England and the empire of which we may be justly proud-the Union Jack- when floated or wherever exposed, has an inspiring effect, there being in it so much of sentiment and meaning for sober thought. In the words of the poet, so beautifully outlined :

The Union Jack.
It's only a small bit of bunting,
It's only an old coloured rag,
Yet thousands have died for its honour And shed their best blood for the flag.
It flutters triumphant o'er ocean As free as the wind and the waves,
And bondsmen from shackles unloosened 'Neath its shadows no longer are slaves.
We hoist it to show our devotion To our King, to our country, and laws, It's the outward and visible emblem Of advancement, and liberty's cause.
You may say its an old bit of bunting, You may call it an old coloured rag,
But freedom has made it majestic And time has ennobled the flag.
Even the colours In the Union Jack, anil you will remember the Union Jack forms part of the Canadian- ensign, has its sentiment and significance, the red indicating courage, white the emblem of purity, and blue the emblem of truth, more strikingly given in the old loyal and familiar song :	' Three cheers for the Red, White
and Blue,' or more sentimental and expressively rendered 'Three cheers for the brave, pure, and true.'
Let me say that lessons such as this, should be deeply impressed upon the mind3 of our Canadian children, particularly at school, so as to have them live lives worthy ®f the ideals of their national flag, and frame the character of our nation by its teaching.
With such natural emotions animating the hearts of our people, one can appreciate the fervid interest taken by each nation in its own national flag, and can realize and account for the associations which cluster about its folds, and are so ardently treasured In the inmost recesses of the human heart. With such feelings of affection for one's country's flag, picture to yourself the heart of that Consul in Rio-Grande-do-sul, destroying the Canadian flag by cutting the heart out °f it-the Canadian coat of arms held by us so dearly and thereby mutilating the Canadian flag completely ! I feel that no punishment, however severe, would be too great for the heartless act he (the Consul) has committed in the matter of the Canadian flag hoisted on *ie ship.' ' M. J. Taylor.' I sincerely hope this government will advise the imperial government to this end.
Kings in their turn display the banner of their kingdoms, over which they reign, and have sway, value them and float them proudly. Picture to yourself, Mr. Speaker, cutting the cross of St. George out of the flag of old England, or the cross of St. Andrew representing Scotland, or the cross of St. Patrick representing Ireland, or the fleur-de-lis from the flag of old France, or even interfering with one star, or one stripe of the star-spangled banner of the United States, would there not be a howl ? Surely they would be heard from in the most emphatic tones. Then are we as Canadians to Mr. KAULBACH.
suffer the ignominy, nay, I must say the. outrage of having the escutcheon or emblem of Canada constituting Canada's flag-cut out of the red fly of the ensign of old England floated on a British ship, commanded by a British master, in a foreign port, by a British consul not knowing his duty, and be silent ? I say certainly not- I must therefore in conclusion, impress upon hon. gentlemen opposite the necessity of making public this matter, and obtaining redress in the manner I have advised.

speechtext:

The hon. gentleman told us that he would have some information to bring before us, but I think there are some facts which have passed into oblivion, and as soon as we have collected the information we shall communicate with the imperial authorities upon this important subject.

speechtext: Before proceeding with the Orders of the Day, I wish to lay upon the table of the House a copy of the memorandum referred to in Col. Smart's letter dated Ottawa, May 19. This memorandum was mislaid at the time the letter was copied, and was inadvertently omitted. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), when asking for this in the House, also asked for the originals of certain other documents and papers, copies of which have been laid before the House. I would say that it is not the practice to lay the originals on the table of the House. But if the hon. gentleman gives any reason why this should be done I am prepared to do it. The hon. gentleman also asked for copies of letters of the 14th and 15th of May from Lieutenant-Colonel Whitley. One of these letters was marked by Lieutenant-Colonel Whitney ' Private ' and the other 'strictly private' therefore I do not feel at liberty to lay them on the table, nor some other letters to which the hon. gentleman referred. These letters are of a personal and confidential character, addressed to me by constituents of *mine, and I decline to lay them on the table.

maintopic: DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD- PRODUCTION OF CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has referred to the request which I made, and announces a principle which is new to me, when he says that the originals of documents of the importance of those I referred to the other

day, should not be communicated to the House. I am not aware that that is the practice of the House. We have an absolute right to see the original of any document to which we have access. It is only for the sake of convenience that copies are made and laid on the table of the House,
1 think there can be no doubt about that.
X am not aware that there is any practice to the contrary. Nor are we obliged, when desirous of seeing documents, to state for what reason we wish to see the originals. Our right to inspect original documents is absolute, and we are not obliged to state why we wish to see them. I would like your ruling upon that point Mr. Speaker. However, I do not think there is any doubt about it. Now, as to the documents marked ' private,' I stated the other day when I made my request to the House, that I considered that no document having reference to the organization of this Scottish regiment could be considered as a private document. The questions which have been raised by what is called the Dundonald affair are matters which concern the entire organization of the militia, and the hon. gentleman's conduct in regard to that organization has been called in question, and also his right to interfere in any way with the organization of a militia regiment. I do not think it is a valid defence to make to the House that wishes to become cognizant of all the circumstances connected with the organization of the regiment, to say that the document is marked ' private,' even ' strictly private.' No document concerning public affairs Is a private document to the extent that communication of that document can be refused to the House. I think that is the rule. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, if I mistake not, a few years ago read a letter which was addressed to him by Reverend Father Le-combe.

A letter which, if my memory serves me right -the matter can easily be verified, I am now speaking of what occurred several years ago-which was addressed by Father Leeombe to the right hon. the Prime Minister, was read by the right hon. gentleman in a discussion which took place in this House during the last preceeding parliament.	.
Sta- WILFRID LAURIER. My hon. friend is altogether mistaken.

At any rate I maintain that we cannot fully inquire into the circumstances of the organization of this regiment and, if I may be allowed to say so, into the charge of interference by the hon. Minister of Agriculture unless we can see these letters, which, although marked ' private,' concern the beginning and organization of this regiment. If these letters are refused us we will be at a disadvantage under which as members of this House we ought not to be placed.

speechtext: < I would point out to my hon. friend that his argument as to the correspondence not being laid on the table of the House has only reference to where the order of the House has issued. In this case there has been no order of the House issued and that contention absolutely falls to the ground. At the same time I do not in any way act upon that argument.

speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture must remember that the hon. Minister of Finance stated that the correspondence which I asked for would all be brought down unless there was something private. What I maintain is that there is nothing private in this connection.

maintopic: DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD- PRODUCTION OF CORRESPONDENCE.
speechtext: I am not speaking of the hon. gentleman's request of the night before last. I am speaking of the original request to have this correspondence laid on the table of the House, a request which was made by some hon. gentlemen of the opposition and which was frankly acceded to by myself and my colleagues, when the letters which are now before the House and which are contained in this printed document were brought down. But, independently altogether of that I may say in the first place to my hon. friend that when an order of the House issues it is an order for copies of the correspondence, and it is only when the request is made and some grounds shown for it that the originals are brought down. I can only suppose that my hon. friend wishes the originals of these letters because he thinks that the copies are not correct. If -the copies are absolutely correct I cannot conceive of any particular purpose in bringing the originals down. I can only say to my hon. friend that I have in my hands the originals of the letters which he refers to. He refers to two memoranda. I only know of one and therefore I can only lay that one on the table, but in regard to the two letters of Colonel Smart and the memorandum that is referred to in the letter I will lay the originals on the table at the present moment in deference to the hon. gentleman's request although I think it is contrary to the usual practice.

Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee on Bill (No. 102) to amend the Shipping Casualties Act, 1901.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I "would like to call the attention of the House to the fact that the change proposed by this Bill is something of the same nature as that which was proposed the other day by my hon. friend (Mr. Prefontaine) when he moved the second reading of Bill (No. 100) entitled ' An Act to amend the Pilotage Act ' to this extent that instead of substituting the authority of the minister he now substitutes the tribunal which is created by the statute of 1901 entitled 1 The Shipping Casualties Act.' The latter Act enacts that:
The minister may direct the principal officer of customs residing at or near the place where such shipping oasualty occurred, if it occurred on or near any of the inland waters of Canada or on or near the coasts of Canada-

I would ask the House to keep better order. We cannot hear a word of what is being said.
Mr. CASGRAIN (reading)-
-but if elsewhere, at or near the place where such witness as aforesaid arrives, or is found, or cian he conveniently examined, or any officer of the government of Canada, whom the minister appoints, or any other person appointed by the minister, to make inquiry respecting such shipping casualty.
In virtue of the statute the person thus appointed or empowered to hold the investigation into the conduct of the master or mate of a ship is also empowered to Impose fines and penalties on the master or mate who is found guilty of infractions of the law or of neglect of duty. By the amendment to this statute it is sought to enlarge the powers of this tribunal so composed, so that the tribunal may be also a tribunal for the trial of pilots. The Bill says, subsection 2 of section 2 :
If, upon a preliminary inquiry, the officer holding it is of opinion that any loss, or damage, or the stranding of any ship, or any loss of life, has been caused by the wrongful act or default of the pilot in charge, or that such pilot has been guilty of any gross act of misconduct or drunkenness, the license of such pilot may be .suspended by such officer until a formal investigation under this Act has been held and a further decision rendered upon the case.
Section 3 adds section 27 to the -Act already existing and it enacts that if the pilot is found guilty by this tribunal bis license

T

may be cancelled, he may be suspended and he may be condemned to a fine.
In any sum not exceeding one-half of the net income he derives from his service as a pilot, based upon his earnings for the previous year.
Mr. Speaker, I really must ask you to maintain order. I do not see how it is that we should be obliged to speak at the top of our voices to be heard on the other side of the House. It is really very fatiguing.

I must say that I have done my best to try and keep order, but it seems that the House has no respect whatever for the chair. The Speaker calls out ' order ' three or four times in succession and nobody seems to pay the slightest attention to it.

This vests this tribunal with large powers and it is taking away from the pilotage authority that is established, especially in the district of Quebec which tries pilots, the authority that it has now, to try them. Of course the penalties To which pilots are subjected are very severe, and they are made more severe by this Bill because not only can they be suspended, but the sentence of the court may be to this extent, that a pilot can be put under a penalty not exceeding one half of the net income he derives from his services as a pilot based upon his earnings for the previous year. Therefore, if a pilot earns $1,000 in a year, he could be fined to the extent of $500. If we were sure that the person appointed by the minister would always be a fit and proper person, probably there could hot be much exception taken to the Bill. But, under this law, the minister has vast power. He may appoint a principal officer of customs or any officer of the government of Canada, or any person, to make preliminary inquiries. I understand that heretofore Captain Spain or Captain Salmon with two nautical assessors have been appointed. I have not the least objection to these two gentlemen or to the assessors who have been appointed hitherto, but at the same time the minister takes power to appoint any officer of the government, and however competent an officer may be to discharge his ordinary duties, when it comes to trying a pilot for neglect of duty or negligence, it is a technical matter which these officials may not be competent to deal with. I would suggest that section 4 limit the minister's authority to the appointment of some person who would be qualified.

Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,
What is the meaning of the expression : ' any person not belonging to a ship ?' It seems a curious expression to use.
It means a person hired especially to act as pilot.
Is the expression taken from any other legislation ?
The Bill was drafted by my department, and submitted to the Department of Justice. It would not mean a pilot engaged, by the year, for instance.
The whole expression : 'any person not belonging to a ship who has the conduct thereof,' seems rather peculiar.
A number of ships trading between the gulf ports and Quebec and Montreal, have pilots who are hired by the year and who act as captains. Would they come under this law ?

This may not be a very happy expression, but I have seen it used in similar legislation. It means a pilot who is in charge of the navigation of the boat at the time, but who is not part of the personnel of the boat.

Then, what about the men who pilot these ships from the gulf ports-thus dispensing with the employment of temporary pilots-but who are engaged by the year ? Being pilots they are employed as captains, and consequently the ship is not obliged to take a pilot.
Then they become masters.
The hon. gentleman said that this Act did not apply to any person hired by the year, and therefore these men would not come under the operation of the law.
They would become masters in that case, and they are provided for in another section.

A pilot is a person who is engaged to navigate a ship for the time being, and who is not on the articles of the ship as the master and the other officers are. If he is engaged to navigate aj ship for a whole year, then he is an officer of that ship, and is on the articles and this Act would not apply to him.
On section 2,

This would permit the government to appoint the inspector of insurance for example or a clerk in the Inland Revenue Department to investigate a shipping casualty, as I understand the effect of the section.

I have retained the same definition as existed in the former Act passed in 1901, and that Act applied to masters, mates and engineers. If the parliament of Canada at the time they passed this

Act had sufficient confidence in the Department of Marine to trust them and to believe that they would appoint a proper officer and if there has been no complaint since this Act was put in operation, not even from those against whom the Act operates, the masters, mates and engineers who are just as important as the pilots, I do not see why there should now be any complaint. But of course X would have no objection to any suggestion to improve the clause.
My only objection was that the clause in its present form, and in its former reading is very comprehensive. It does not limit the appointment to skilled persons in any way.
The original Act did not either.

X know, and of course the original Act is open to the same criticism. However the responsibility will be always on the government to appoint the person. I suppose that is the only justification for the clause if it has any justification.
X would suggest that this subsection be amended by adding the word ' skilled ' before the word ' person ' in the third line, so that the section would read, ' or any skilled person.'
Define what you mean by ' skilled person.'

Skilled in this particular matter, skilled to make preliminary inquiries respecting such shipping casualties. The word ' skilled ' is defined by the words coming after, skilled in such matters as the Bill relates to.

If a person other than a customs officer is appointed, would you exact that he be skilled, and who is to pass on his qualification ? If this was adopted I am quite sure it would nullify the effect of the Act, because every time there would be a dispute about the skill of the man appointed. If you want to afford the shipping interest the necessary guarantee, you must trust some one, and it is not likely that the officers of the Department of Marine would appoint a man not able to carry on an investigation. If an investigation was not carried on properly the department would suffer because the shipping people would very quickly make a public complaint. There has been no complaint since 1901 when this Act went into operation. Capt. Salmon who is the head of the department as regards masters and mates has always taken care to have the best assesssors he could find to help him in the investigation and the investigations have proven very satisfactory every time.
How are the assessors apppointed, under the law ?

Under the law, section 9 of the Act, and the section shows that every precaution is taken.

I would call the attention of the minister to a matter which is of some importance in the county of Jacques Cartier, and with which he is as well acquaint-168
ed as I am. He knows there is, behind the island of Montreal, a stream known as Back river or Riviere des Prairies, which passes in front of the parish of Ste. Genevieve. On one side is the parish of Ste. Genevieve, a populous parish. This is on the island of Montreal, and is frequented by a considerable number of people from the city of Montreal during the summer. Opposite is the parish of He Bizard, which island is nine miles long and a mile or two wide, and lying in the lake of Two Mountains. This would be a very important place for a summer resort if it were more easily accessible. These two parishes, lying thus face to face on the Back river, are about eight miles from Ste. Anne's and in the lake of Two Mountains. The lake of Two Mountains empties into Riviere des Prairies, which passes in front of the parish of Ste. Genevieve and He Bizard, about three miles from the lake. There would be uninterrupted navigation from the lake of Two Mountains down to these two parishes from Ste. Anne's, and consequently from Vaudreuil, Oka, Hudson, Como and, in fact, all the ports of the Ottawa river, but for a small obstruction just at the point where the lake of Two Mountains empties into the Back river. There is a small rapid-in fact it is called Little Rapid-and were it not for this there would be uninterrupted navigation between the lake and these two parishes. I have always been under the impression-and that impression is general among the people down there-that this obstruction could be removed at a comparative trifling cost. What 1 would like the Minister of .Marine and Fisheries to do, if the cost is really trifling, is to have this work of removal of this obstruction done out of this vote. He might perhaps have the obstruction examined by one of the engineers of his department and, if the expense is not very great, and a channel of 15 or 20 feet could toe had by doing a little work, the two parishes I have mentioned wrould be benefited, and, in an indirect way, so would the whole of the city of Montreal. Access could be had to these parishes to the lake at all times. As we have no railway communication at Site. Genevieve or lie Bizard, I think this modest i t quest deserves the attention of the minister. I hope he will look into the matter and have the work done, if it is not found to be too expensive.

Has the hon. gentleman (Mr. 'Monk) any idea of wliat it would
cost ?

No ; but I have often been told by people from the place, not experts, of course, but people having some local knowledge, that the shallow water, where it flows through the Little Rapids-it can scarcely be called a rapid-extends over a very short distance, and that a little blasting would remove the obstruction and allow free access to these two parishes from the



lake-in fact, would make these river ports. My hon. friend understands, of course, that that is a matter of some importance.

I have no objection to having the investigation made, and if the removal of the obstruction comes within the purview of this vote I will attend to it.
Tidal service, including salary of assistant clerk beyond salary of $400, notwithstanding *anything in the Civil Service Act, $22,500.
When was the steamer " Gulnare,' which is used in this service, purchased, and what was the cost ?
The steamer was bought a vear ago last November at a cost of 826,000.
The minister was not very accurate in his estimates. I notice when this matter was up for discussion before, he said the salaries would amount to about $2,400 ; now they are over $6,000.
The pay-list of the officers and crew for the last year amounts to $6,513.73. That is what was expended.
Was this a second-hand boat or a new one ?

The boat was built for the imperial government, and specially fitted up for this kind of work. She was leased by the imperial government and bought from the owners. Sfre was built of steel, and is nine years old.

We had a case yesterday in which it was shown that a boat had to be disposed of on account of her age. It seems to be the policy of the minister to purchase these old second-hand boats from time to time. May I ask the minister when he is about to invest in a boat, what steps are taken ? Is a specification prepared of the kind of boat that is required, and are tenders invited as to what such a boat will cost ? Or does the minister simply go out and. hear of some person having a boat and buy it at their own price ? What is the policy of the department in this respect ?

In this case there is no fixed policy. Iu this case the department wanted a boat, and bought one in April, 1902, before I took charge of the department. This boat was offered to the department, and Mr. Douglas Stephen, inspector of government steamers, was asked to make a report on her, which report I now have before me'. I may say thab the boat cost originally $85,000, and it was bought for $36,000 on the recommendation of Dr. Dawson who was in charge of the service. It was the only ship available for this kind of work.

It seems to me that some person comes along, whenever they hear that the minister wishes to buy a boat, and offer it at their own price. Then some officer of the department comes in, and if he Mr. MONK.
thinks it is right the boat is taken at that price. I do not think there is any other department that proceeds on those lines. If the department wants a boat there is a procedure laid down. Plans are prepared and tenders invited. If that is not always the case, it should be. But the minister, in disregard of business methods, looks around, makes up his mind that he must have a boat, and then and there if he sees one that suits him, he gives the vendor his own price. Was this the first price asked by the vendor, or did the minister succeed in beating him down ?

The purchase was made, as I have said, before I took charge of the department. An explanation was given. I am informed, a year ago, and was considered satisfactory. The boat was built specially for the imperial government for the same kind of work that she is doing at the present time. She cost $85,000, and was bought for $36,000, after the owners had asked $42,000.

Then there must have been something radically wrong with the boat, if she cost only $85,000 six years before, and was sold for less than half that sum. What explanation can the minister give as to why the boat-I presume she was an iron bottom boat-was sacrificed at that figure ?

She was in perfect condition, and the reason we were able to buy her at such a low price was that the imperial government had no more use for her. She could not be used for any other purpose, because she was built specially for that purpose.
Are there any vessels being constructed now for his department ?
Yes. The ' Canada ' is being constructed by Vickers. Maxim & Son. She is a cruiser, and was launched on the 14th of this month.
What is the prospective cost of that steamer ?

I forgot to mention that another one is being constructed by the Poison Company, Toronto, a cruiser destined for the lakes to replace the ' Petrel,' which was not found.fast enough to compete with the American boats.
What is the estimated cost of the two boats ?
I will be ready to give all the details regarding these two boats when the item comes up.
Approximately.
In the case of the boat that is being built in the old country, were the plans prepared by the department ; also were plans prepared for the boat that Is being constructed by the Poison Company ?
The plans were prepared in the department and submitted to experts and prices were asked on these plans.

When the bon. minister comes down again with some further estimates will he be good enough to give the tenders which were submitted for the two boats, first, for the one constructed in the old country, and second, for the one constructed by the Poisons ? No one can find fault if, after the preparation of plans and specifications, these were openly advertised and tenders invited. In that case it would be a business proposition. But, on the other hand, if the department simply invited these gentlemen in the old country and the Poisons to construct boats and then to fix their own prices, it is a different proposition.
I will have all the information.
Is the Poison boat to be built in the time limited ?

She is going to be delivered within a week.

Marine biological station, $3,000.

This is a new experiment not inaugurated by me, but it is an expenditure which began in 1898 when an amount of $7,000 was placed in the estimates for a marine biological station, $5,000 for providing a floating station, and $2,000 for providing for the maintenance and support of such station and the payment of salaries. It was found that $2,000 a year was not sufficient to meet all the expenses in connection with the maintenance of the station and the salaries of the university 1681
professors who have the station in charge, and they called upon me,' and I agreed to increase the amount to $3,000. That amount was voted in the supplementary estimates last year. Last year the station was located at Malpeque. I have not yet received the report of the professors in charge.
What is the station for ?

These scientific people make special researches into and studies of fish life. They are professors of the different universities at Toronto and elsewhere. It was at their request that this biological station was. established in 1898 and it has been maintained since that time.
Is that the station at which Professor Ramsay Wright was experimenting last year ?
Yes.
Has he sent in his report to the department ?
No.
I think it would be a very interesting report if it were sent in, and if the government are spending money in that direction, the result of the experiments should be given to us.

It is proposed to issue it.
Mr. HACIvETT. Might I ask who are the gentlemen in addition to Professor Prince who are connected with this biological station ?	*
All the professors from Toronto, McGill and Laval universities.
What is the object of having this biological station ?
Would the hon. gentleman give us a resume of what he has just read. In the first place we do not understand a word of what he has said except his reference to Malpeque oysters.

1 thought I had it very clearly at the beginning and that it was only for the pleasure of having me read the list of subjects mentioned in the report that the request for further information was made of me. If I say a few words I am called down, and if I Say too much I am called down. What I said was that these scientists are making a special study of fish life in its different phases. They are studying the oyster, the taking of which is becoming an important industry and they are also devoting their attention to other questions affecting fish life.
I understand the hon. minister to say that there is no report of last year's operations.
We have not received it yet.

Is it private ?
Salaries and expenses of cattle inspection, $3,600.
What is this cattle inspection ?

This vote is to pay the officers whom the department has charged specially to see that cattle are shipped in compliance with the regulations as to cattle space, food, &c. There are two in Montreal and one at St. John.
Could the hon. gentleman give ns the salaries paid to these gentlemen ?

Geo. H. Pope, formerly of Belleville, gets $1,000 ; and H. Delorme $1,000. They are the inspectors at Montreal. The expenses of the inspectors were $207.72. Thos. Bucltley, the inspector at St. John, has a salary of $800. There was paid to Mr. Hunter, at Halifax, $67.15, and H. P. Walsh, Charlottetown, $500.
Do I understand that the cattle exported at these different ports are inspected by these gentlemen ?
Yes.
Do they make a report?
Yes. It is published in the report of the department.
What salary is paid to O. G. Y. Spain ?
$2,000 a year.
I see the government paid $100 for a fur-lined coat for this gentleman. Can he not provide his own clothing ?

That amount has been refunded by Captain Spain. It was on a trip to Newfoundland and he thought he was authorized on account of the severity of the winter to make that expenditure. He refunded the amount when he was called on to do so.
The Auditor General's Report does not say that it was refunded.
I am informed that the amount was refunded since that report.
Where is the coat ?
I suppose he has [DOT]got it himself ; he paid for it.

Is this officer still in the employ of the department ? Do you allow your officers to go around buying what they please ? Do I understand the minister to say that this man whom the government paid $100 for a furlined coat for, can charge his ordinary clothing to the country ? Is
[DOT]5293

that the minister's view of what his duty to the public is ? It was only on account of the vigilance of that most excellent officer, the Auditor General, that attention was called to this, and the country saved this amount. And the Auditor General's services are to be dispensed with, because hie can no longer put up with the way in which his decisions are overruled by this government. It seems to me that the Minister of Marine should give a pledge to this committee that this man Spain should be dismissed from the service ; a man who has such an idea of his duty as a public officer.

In justification of Captain Spain I am informed by my officials that he was authorized to buy this coat, on account of the extended trip he was taking ; and when it was discovered it was illegal, he kept the coat and refunded the money.

What officer authorized him to buy this coat, because he happened to be going to Newfoundland? The climate of Newfoundland is not so much different from the climate of Canada as to necessitate the government buying a coat for him, any [more than if he were going to any other part of Canada.

I am informed that it was during a severe winter when he was snowed in for eight or ten days, and he asked authorization from the minister, and the minister gave him the authority or some employee implied that he was authorized from the minister to buy a coat. He used the coat, and when the department was called upon to reimburse the amount as an illegal expenditure, he reimbursed it.
Where does that amount appear as being reimbursed.
It will appear in the next Auditor General's Report.

Had this man no coat at all ? It seems rather strange that in Canada, a man occupying the position of Captain Spain would not be in possession of a furlined coat. Men who receive less salaries than he, have furlined coats. It is only a small matter I admit, but it is a straw which shows how the wind is blowing. It is a most outrageous thing. WTho was minister when this authorization was given to Spain to buy a coat-I am reminded by one of my hon. friends that this $100 fer the fcoat, is just the price the minister got for that timber limit which he sold to his friends. It took that $100 to supply a coat for an officer.

One hundred dollars from the minister's point of view is no great matter, when they are frittering away millions. But it is a considerable amount in the eyes of the hard working farmers of this country. Here is a minister of the Crown
who sells timber off 100 acres of land for just the amount of money that one of his officials is giving for a furlined coat. The principle underlying this transaction is what I object to.
It was not principle; it was fur that was underlying it.

If the government keep on at this rate taking taxes out of the people for such purposes, there will not be much fur left on the taxpayers. The right hon. the Prime Minister tells us that they are a business government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) sitting beside you is *your joker.

When the Prime Minister tells me that this is a business government he is not only deceiving me but he is deceiving the whole country. I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Macdonald) if any business man wrould sell the timber on a 100 acres of land without asking for tenders.
On the recommendation of a member of parliament.

I can see that he might be deceived by a member of parliament, but if he were a business man he would not be. I have no doubt of Mr. Spain's ability. Mr. Spain no doubt is a very worthy officer and I understand howr Mr. Spain could be misled into this trouble, but do you think Mr. Chairman, that Mr. Spain would have refunded that money if it had not been for the Auditor General. I was very much grieved to hear that that gentleman is going to resign.
Do you mean the minister ?

No. no ; I mean the Auditor General. There is no trouble about retaining the minister. He has got a good fat job and there is no trouble about his conscientious scruples forcing him to resign as long as he gets the salary he now gets. I see from the Auditor General's Report that he got an advance of $250 for travelling expenses.
He can buy a coat with that.

He can explain what he did with it when I get through. I think I would retain office if I got the salary he does, and when we ask for explanations he does not know anything about the matters in question and simply reads the reports

but reads them in such a way that no one can understand him. I certainly cannot understand him. This official spent $100 for a fur-lined coat. I wish the hon. gentleman who leads this government to stop writing for a few moments and in order that X may ask him if he thinks that this is a business transaction. In looking over the Auditor General's Report I find gentlemen travelling in the Northwest buying eider-down quilts at $25 and eider-down pillows at $8 or $10.
They had been on the straw before.

It is all very well to laugh but it is a serious matter that the public of Canada has to pay for these things. I would like to know, if any hon. gentleman representing a rural constituency in this House should submit these questions to the electorate how many of the electors, men and women who work hard to pay the exorbitant taxation required for the support of this reckless administration, could state what an eider-down quilt is. Just fancy, eider-down quilts for gentlemen rolling around the Northwest country and three or four satchels for one gentleman and $3.p0 for a leather pocket-book for one official. I ask the leader of the government if he thinks that is a business transaction.

House in Committee on Bill (No. 29) to incorporate the Canadian Credit, Indemnity and Guaranty Company.-Mr. Guthrie.
Mr. GUTHRIE moved to add the following words to clause 2 :
In case any of the provisional directors resign or decline to act at any time, their places may he filled by the remaining directors appointing another or others in their place, but it shall not be necessary for them to do so. The quorum shall consist of the majority of provisional directors from time to time in office and acting.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: This is rather an unusual clause to introduce at this stage. This Bill was considered by the Banking and Commerce Committee yesterday, and this seems to me a very important amendment to bring up after the Bill was considered by the committee. I think the promoters should ask to have the Bill sent back to the committee for further consideration and let the committee deal with it.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext:
There was some discussion in the committee yesterday as to the number of provisional directors who should form a quorum. The difficulty is that there Mr. COCHRANE.
are eleven provisional directors and it requires six to form a quorum. They are all very prominent and busy men and it is questionable if six can be got together. This amendment only gives power to appoint new provisional directors in case any of those named decline to act or resign. If they do, the remaining directors can appoint others to fill their places, but a majority is still required to form a quorum. This does not affect the working out of the matter in any way, but still leaves a majority necessary before anything can be done.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: It was pointed out in the committee that it was difficult to get a majority of the directors present and therefore it was desirable, if any should resign- which I suppose is intended by this Act- that a majority of those remaining should form a quorum. But the danger, I see is to whom are they to resign and how are they to resign. The amendment provides for their failing or refusing to act, but what evidence will we have of that ? The work done by the provisional board may be all upset by some irregularity or some difficulty in finally determining whether these directors have declined to act or to whom they are to resign. I would prefer that the number of provisional directors should be reduced instead of making this provision, as I see a good many difficulties in working it out.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: I think the resignation in writing to the other provisional directors would be a sufficient resignation on which to act.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext:
It seems of little use to refer a Bill to a select committee, if action of this kind is to be taken immediately on the return of the Bill to the House. I do not think the point is well taken. I find that the names of the provincial directors include the following :
James Joseph Kenny, John Woodburn Langmuir, John Fitzallen Ellis, William Stone, Alexander Archibald Allan, Phineas Hophni Burton, Peleg Howland, William Kirkpatrick McNaught, and Robert Bryson Osborne, all of the city of Toronto, and John Roaf Barber, of Georgetown, in the county of Halton.
All these gentlemen are in Toronto, excep't Mr. Barber, who is in Georgetown, very near to Toronto, and who spends about as much time in Toronto as he does in Georgetown. Practically these provisional directors all live in one city. I do not see why there should be any difficulty in getting a majority of them together. Yesterday when the question was before the Banking and Commerce Committee we were firm on the point that a majority should constitute a quorum and I object to the change.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: It still leaves it a majority. Some of these gentlemen, I understand, are not very anxious to act in the work of provisional directors.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: But surely they would be willing to meet in order to make the proceedings regular. I agree with the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) that there might be a difficulty if a notification by one provisional director to all the others were counted a sufficient withdrawal. But I approve of the Bill being referred back to the Committee on Banking and Commerce. I understand that there is to be a meeting early next week, and the Bill can be considered in the House again. There is no danger of it being lost through any delay of this kind.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: I would not object to that if there was anything material in it. But, as we know, the duties of provisional directors are very slight-merely to meet and organize and get subscriptions. If any one of the board does not desire to do the work and resigns, addressing his resignation to the provisional directors of the company, surely that ought to overcome any irregularity. At all events, I suspect that the gentlemen who seek the amendment are the only ones who would involve themselves. I do not think there is much in the objection.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: How many directors are there ?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: Eleven.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: But if you drop two, a majority would be five, and surely that number can be got to take part in the organization of the company.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CREDIT, INDEMNITY AND GUARANTY COMPANY.
speechtext: At present we want six. But, if two drop, five would be enough. It is a minor matter, I think.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, before this Bill is read the second time, if the promoter of the Bill (Mr. Russell) is present I would like to have some explanation as to why the company have not proceeded to organize this bank before asking us to grant this extension of time. Last year we granted nine bank charters and I am not aware that more than one of these banks actually went into operation. It seems to me that it is quite unnecessary for us to proceed with the granting of bank charters year after year unless some action is to be taken. I do not think it is a wise thing to hold these charters over from year to year without taking some action, and I would have hoped that the promoter of the Bill would have been present to have given the House some reason why the purposes of the Bill had not been accomplished, why action had not been taken and the bank actually put into operation.

The hon. member (Mr. Russell) who is in charge of this Bill, is out of the House just now. I have charge of it in his absence. [DOT] When this matter came up before the House a few days ago, satisfactory explanations were given at the time as to the reason why the promoters had not gone forward with the organization of this bank during the year. This charter has not been held over from year to year. They are men of means and I have no doubt whatever that if the House will consent to the Bill which is now before it, the work of organization will be carried forward speedily. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), when this matter was before the House, expressed his satisfaction with the reason which had compelled this company to delay organizing, and I am sure that my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) will not insist at the present time upon throwing any obstacles in the way of carrying this measure to completion.

If I am assured that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who resides in Halifax, the head office, I presume, of this intended bank, was satisfied, I would in no way desire to press any

further objection, but I must say, as I understand that the Alliance Bank is simply an amalgamation of a number of other banks, that I fail to see wherein the condition of the money market could have any effect whatever in preventing the object of the promoters being carried out.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

speechtext: This, I may say, is a somewhat extraordinary Bill. We are incorporating a company to do work in South America. I have no file of the Bill, and I am not aware whether it has been printed. It is not marked as having been printed. I think we ought to have some knowledge as to what the Bill is.

It is not marked as printed on mine, and I presume mine must rule, because this is the notice that has been given to us. My hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) says it is not distributed. Mr. CALVEuT. Mr. Speaker, when I asked the permission of the House to present the petition for this Bill, I endeavoured to give an explanation and it was agreed to both by the right hon. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understand that the services of a great many of the light keepers above Montreal have been dispensed with. After fifteen or twenty years service the minister simply told these men to walk, giving them a few months notice. Is that fair treatment for men who have been in the service of the country for many years ? Is it the intention to give them some compensation.
