speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Does the minister include in that comparative statement the cost of the steamer '-Scout,' that is scouting around the lakes with a large crew on board ?
Mr.	PREFONT AINE.	The steamer
would have to be maintained all the same to look after the buoy service,

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The lights were there for many years and we had no steamer to look after them ; nor did we have to maintain a factory and employ about 100 men up there at Prescott in connection with this carbide which is made here at Ottawa by a company in which some of the cabinet ministers are stockholders.
Well, what if they are ?	'

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I may say that this system of lighting with carbide was started
simply for the purpose of purchasing' carbide from a company in Ottawa, promoted by members of this government. My hon. friend has started a factory at Prescott, having purchased a property there without a vote of this House, that I know of. I never heard of a vote to purchase property there for that purpose, and I knew nothing of the project until I was in Prescott the other day and saw something like one hundred men working there on property purchased at large expense. We have not been asked to purchase the property or told that the government were going to start a factory to make tanks to hold acetylene gas. So far as I know this gas,
I would not have it on any property I own. You can hardly read a paper, but you see accounts of explosions of this gas, yet the government, because some of its members are engaged in the manufacture of the carbide, purchase a property, start a factory and employ some one hundred men.
What does the hon. gentleman mean ? What kind of a factory ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is my hon. friend doing in Prescott in the Wiser distillery works ?
Does he mean we are manufacturing carbide at Prescott ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, manufacturing iron tanks to hold the gas you make from carbide. Am I not correct ?
Somewhat correct.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where did the minister get the authority to get that property and start this factory ? We have never heard of it in parliament, but there is the factory to-day running and manufacturing these things that might be made at the Kingston locomotive works or the Kingston boiler works. But my hon. friend has purchased a property there and has one hundred men employed, running a manufacturing industry, competing with other Canadian manufacturers.

The explanation is very simple. $35,000 was voted last year to purchase the Prescott property. I know nothing personally of the property itself. I know that the property was considered good value at $40,000, but we managed to buy it at $26,000, or thereabouts, after the amount had been v.oted by parliament last year. It was considered to be in the interest of navigation and of aids to navigation to establish a station at that point. I am awfully sorry that we should be called down for having done a thing which is in the interests of navigation on the lakes. If we had thought that we would be reproached for it we would have put the money elsewhere, and then we would not have, been accused of having done anything

wrong towards the country. Another time I suppose we will consult the gentlemen who represent the district. We intend to put a station at Parry Sound, but if it is objected to of course we will put it somewhere else, and will have all the supplies necessary for the lights whether acetylene gas or any other gas, kept at a place where no objection will be raised. I am very sorry when we have established such a station at this point for the sake of improving aids to navigation on the upper lakes, and between Montreal and Kingston, that we should have been accused of having done something that is wrong. The whole question came before the House last year and was approved of. The explanations were all given at the time and we went on with the project just as we have been going on with the shipyard at Sorel. We do not find any kick about the shipyard at Sorel. Every one is satisfied in Quebec; they think it is right that it should be established there and worked there, and that it is doing good work. The fact of the matter is that we are being asked every day to have everything done at the yards there. Instead of giving out contracts for the building of ships and boats in private shipyards, we are asked to do it at Sorel where we have the men and facilities necessary to do the work in the interests of the country. If these gentlemen are not satisfied with the establishment of the station at Prescott, I am very sorry. We are not going to abolish the station which has got to work. It is useful and is going to be worked in the best interests of the province of Ontario in spite of the hon. gentlemen on the other side, who do not think this should be done.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would like the hon. gentleman to point to me in the estimates of last year or in the debates of last year, where $35,000 was voted and one word said about purchasing a property at Prescott to start an industry for manufacturing tanks to hold this gas. The first I heard of it was when I was in Prescott and saw the place. I do not represent the town of Prescott or that district, but I do say that this expenditure for lighting the River St. Lawrence under this system, including the cost and maintenance of the crew of the steamer ' Scout,' will be largely in excess of the cost of the other system. Under the old system I could stand at Gananoque, and see the three lights looming well, but under this system they, are like little stars.

There are people who cannot see the light. When it is so bright it blinds them. When you have a five candle power light, they can see it, but when it is a fifteen or twenty power light of course it puts them in the shade and they are nowhere.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do say and will maintain that the government had no right to

v
dismiss the faithful and efficient servants who had been employed there for twenty years, and to throw them on the world giving them two or three months' notice. The government had no right to start this manufacturing industry at Prescott without asking parliament. I never heard in the debate, nor can it be pointed out in the records of last year that it was the intention of. parliament to vote this money for the establishment of this factory. I want the minister to point it out. He made the statement that $35,000 was voted last year to purchase this property. Will he point out one word in the estimates or in the debates to show that ?
Was it before the minister came into the department or since, that this purchase of land was made ?

The purchase was made last year after the vote was taken by parliament. I have not the vote before me, but I will have it in a moment. A vote of $180,000 was asked, and this included, I think, the sum of $35,000 to establish a station at Prescott, including the purchase of a property there. The property instead of costing $35,000, has cost only $20,000. At the time we calculated it might cost us $35,000. The price asked was $40,000, so I do not think there is enough in this transaction to kill the government or even a very humble member of the government.

Was any explanation given to the House last year that $35,000 of this $180,000 was being voted for the purchase of that property ?
Mr. -PREFONTAINE. I have sent for the statute.
Under what head will we find that discussed last year ?

Commencing at page P- 47 of the Auditor General's Report there is a resume of the expenditure on lights above Montreal. Now the lights on the St. Lawrence are of course counted among those above Montreal and in looking through this I can find no reference to the purchase of this property. Perhaps the minister can tell us where it is.

On page 31 of the Statutes of 1903. Lighthouse and coast survey.
Further amount for construction and aids to navigation, including the purchase and equipment of boats for sweeping channels . . . and the substitution of compressed gas for oil as illuminant for lighthouses, increasing the power of lights below Montreal and the establishment of a buoy depot for the upper lakes, $180,000.

Surely the minister does not call this the establishment of a buoy depot where they are manufacturing pipes ?
*
They are not manufacturing any thing of the sort.
What is being manufactured at Prescott.
The are manufacturing gas. Some one the other side said so. They are full of it.
Full of what.

Gas. What is being made there is everything that is necessary for keeping the lights in operation. repairing the appliances, filling the bouys, &c. That is the work done at this station which before was done, either in private establishments or at Montreal or elsewhere. Instead of that we thought, seeing the increase of necessities for better aids to navigation, that it was better that all these things should be under the control of the department. That is why the station was established. There is no gas manufactured there, there are no holders manufactured there except for repairs that may be necessary in connection with the working of the buoys.
As I understand the acetylene gas is made in this way : There are certain iron receptacles made for the holding of this carbide.
They are not made there. At this depot they are doing everything necessary to maintain the lights and the buoys on the upper St. Eawrence.

In an acetylene gas plant there is an iron receptacle into which this carbide is introduced and the gas is produced by moisture and is then conveyed by pipes and becomes an illuminating power. We know that the carbide is not manufactured there. It is manufactured at two or three different places, at Ottawa and also at St. Catharines, I think the same company is interested in both concerns, and it is quite well known that the Minister of Public Works is a large stockholder in at least one concern. There is no harm in that but it is a well known fact that Hon. Mr. Sutherland is one of the promoters of that industry. The use of acetylene gas is quite popular in Ontario, although in some places it is not popular by reason of the explosions that occur in connection with it. Am I to understand from the minister that in all the lighthouses on the great lakes, the present system of lighting by oil is to be dispensed with and carbide introduced instead ?

I could not say that off-hand. There are some lights where it is in the interest of the service that acetylene gas should be used, because it gives a mueh stronger light, and there are other places where the oil lamps will be kept. It is a technical question which comes within the province of the officer in charge
of the lights. I may say that almost all of these changes have been asked for by the shipping interests. As regards the acetylene gas, I know nothing particularly as to who manufactures this carbide. I understand there are two companies, one in St. Catharines, controlled entirely by Mr. Willson, and I understand there is another in Ottawa; these two control the market. The factory in Ottawa is controlled by the Messrs, Bronson, of Ottawa, Mr. Cranueil and Mr. Willson and others. I deny that one of the members of the cabinet is a director of the company.

Is the Mr. Willson, who
i.s interested in the one at St. Catharines, the same Mr. Willson woh is interested in the one at Ottawa ?

Yes. From information I have received, the company in St. Catharines is not able to furnish the quantity of carbide asked for. Then there remains this company in Ottawa which is selling all the carbide it can produce to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and other concerns, and the price we pay is the same as is paid by these companies, which buy a larger quantity than we do. The department has no interest whatever in favouring any one company or another. If another company would offer the carbide at a lower price, the department would buy from it.
Do I understand that some of these lighthouse keepers have been dispensed with altogether ?
Yes.
Then at the expiration of the time during which the machines are supposed to run. it will be necessary for a man to reload them ?
No. We have a machine now which is loaded for six months or a year. ' All that is necessary is that it should be visited now and then to see whether the apparatus is in good order and condition.

Then, as there is no caretaker in the building, any one evil disposed could obtain entrance and put the whole arrangement out of gear. And if there should be a wreck, there is no lighthouse keeper to assist the stranded vessel. And if anything should go wrong with the machine, there is no one to set it right.

These changes have been approved by the marine associations and shipping interests all over. \ can produce many letters to show that these interests are very grateful to the department for having adopted this means of giving better aid to navigation. I do not claim credit for this new departure, t found the experiments going on, and after

they proved satisfactory, I thought it my duty to continue the system.
How does the hon. gentleman purchase the property at present ? What has he paid for it and how did he arrive at a valuation ?

The property was valued at $40,000. We did not disclose who wanted to purchase and the price came down to $35,000. We thought it could be bought cheaper and we employed an agent from the city of Ottawa. The politics of this man I do not know, but I am inclined to think he is a Conservative, and we thought that by employing him we could dispel the suspicion that the government wanted the property. We_ succeeded in getting the property at $20,500 instead of $35,000 and we paid about $500 commission.
What arrangement has the minister made with the acetylene gas company for the supply of the carbide, and what period does it cover ?
We buy the carbide at $65 a ton, which is the ordinary price paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
How long does the agreement last ?
There is no agreement. We buy at the market price.
Then when you have all these arrangements made and are using the acetylene light over your whole system, these gentlemen put up the price.
The Canadian Pacific Railway would be in the same position.

I venture to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway does not go into any such bargain. When the Canadian Pacific Railway make a bargain, they see that they do not run the risk of being cornered at the end of the year. I do not think it is right for the minister to bring the Canadian Pacific Railway into this discussion. I am not here to defend the Canadian Pacific Railway or to represent that company, but I am here representing the people of Canada and the constituency for which I am elected ; and when I ask the hon. minister for information, I have the right to get an answer which does not bring in the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am not objecting to the use of the acetylene gas, because I believe it is a light that is going to stay and I hope it will prove much better than what was heretofore used. But what I say is that the government ought to take precautions against being cornered by the people who control the acetylene gas. The government ought to have some arrangement with these people of a permanent character.
Mr. PREFONTAINlEt My department and the government can hardly be blamed Mr. PREFONTAINE.
if they have acted with as great care as that shown by the large private companies. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have fitted up cars at very great expense to burn acetylene gas, and fitted them up so that they will not burn anything else. And the company buy their carbide from the Ottawa Carbide Company at the same price that the government pay. I do not know what the arrangement of the Canadian Pacific Railway with the Carbide Company may be, but I know that we buy the carbide on the market. And if the company wants to charge us a higher price we can go elsewhere. I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) is in a position to tell us what the nature of the contract made by the Canadian Pacific Railway with the Ottawa Carbide Company is, and, if he will do so, perhaps we may be able to make the same contract. At present, though we have made no contract, we are buying carbide at the same price as the Canadian Pacific Railway, $65 a ton. Though we have gone to some expense to provide the apparatus to use this gas, we have not spent as much as the Canadian Pacific Railway in fitting up their cars for the same purpose. So, I think I have a right to say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) has no business to reproach the department for acting as we have done. And even if he tries to divide his responsibility as a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway in making the same kind of a contract that we have made, I think that the people generally Mull not consider that we have been guilty of a great crime.

I do not seek to divide my responsibility as between the Canadian Pacific Railway and this House. My responsibility as a member of this House is here.
I am not here to say whether the Canadian Pacific Railway has made a good or a bad bargain, but I am here to criticise the item under discussion. I say that if the government are going to large expense to change the system of lighting-to which, mind you,
I do not object at all-they must keep in view the fact that the carbide, as I understand it, is controlled by one company.
It is manufactured all over the world.
There is not even a patent on it.
It is practically controlled by one company.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) says that it cannot be manufactured by anybody who chooses to take up that line of business ?

The Standard Oil Company give exactly the same answer as the minister has just given. They say there is no objection to anybody else going into the oil business-that there is no monopoly in the oil business.

There is a great deal of difference. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) as a business roan can defend his proposition that there is a similarity between the Standard Oil Company and the concerns that produce carbide. The Standard Oil Company have bought all the sources of supply, while the carbide industry is an open one in which any one can engage.

I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Prefontaine) endorse so completely the statement I made in the House when the Minister of Finance brought in his Standard Oil legislation the other day. I stated, and the minister of Finance contradicted me, that the new oil duties were simply playing into the hands of the Standard Oil Company, because they had or would have control of the output. The Minister of Finance and others on that side said that I was talking nonsense, but now the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries tells us that the Standard Oil Company own all the oil in the world, and that there is no analogy between the production of carbide and the production of oil. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries goes further than X did. I said that the Standard Oil Company would ultimately control the supply, but the minister says that they do control it. I am confident that I state a fact when I say that the production of carbide is practically a monopoly. I have no accusation to make against any men who are interested in that manufacture. They have a perfect right to engage in it and to make all the money they can out of it. But the government, in making these expensive changes to adopt the new system of lighting should take into account the fact that the production of carbide is practically a monopoly.
Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ?
Yes.
If there is a monopoly-though I do not admit it-and if the hon. gentleman has admitted that there is a monopoly in the oil industry-
I did not admit it, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Prefontaine) stated it.

But that is the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Osier's) argument. He says that the tariff brought down will not benefit the people, because the Standard Oil Company controls the whole trade and will use these duties for its own purposes. It would appear, then, according to the hon. gentleman's argument that it is simply a question of whether we shall face the difficulty of a monopoly in oil or a monopoly in carbide.

The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is a little mixed, or else I am very dense. I did not say that the Standard
Oil Company now had a monopoly, but that it would acquire a monopoly in Canada as it had elsewhere. The minster himself stated absolutely that the Standard Oil Company had a monopoly.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) would allow me. I would like to ask him a question. He stated that the manufacture of carbide was a monopoly
I say that practically carbide is a monopoly. *
Will the hon. gentleman explain what he means by that ?
Practically it is in the hands of a very few.
Does the hon. gentleman know the nature of the monopoly of which he speaks ?
It is of the same nature as the Standard Oil Company-the production is in the hands of a few companies.
Is the hon. gentleman quite sure of that ?
I think so, yes.

I think the hon. gentleman is in error. I know nothing about the internal workings, and so may be in error myself. But I have heard the statement made, and I believe it to be correct, that the patentee of the process is a Mr. Willson of this city. I suppose he patented it in various parts of the world. He is not manufacturing I presume all over the world, but like other persons who have inventions, he sells territory, and probably either retains a royalty or gets something for the sale of the territory. That is a different thing from saying that he controls the market price at which it may be sold. Now the information is easily obtainable, I suppose that gentleman lives in this city, and we could ascertain by telephone whether he controls the selling price. If he does not control the selling price, then there is competition. If this carbide is manufactured throughout the world, then there is competition, and if it happened that manufacturers in Canada should seek to impose high prices upon the people of Canada, then this material could be brought in from other parts of the world where it is manufactured. Unless the hon. gentleman says that one man or one syndicate controls the output and regulates the price so that they can put it up or down, his theory of a monopoly amounts to nothing.
I think the hon. gentleman quite understands a monopoly.
I want the hon. gentleman to explain his argument.

I am speaking quite frankly, because I know nothing about the gentlemen interested in this carbide, and 'have no

interest in it. But if a patent is sold for the manufacture of carbide in Canada, that patent carries with it, as in almost every other case, this right, that if it is manufactured in the United States they cannot come into Canada and .sell it here. That is almost the invariable condition of a patent that is sold anywhere. If you sell a patent in Canada for the manufacture of an article and you sell the patent in England for the manufacture of the same article, the first and primary condition is that no goods manufactured in Canada can be sold in England under that patent.

The hon. gentleman will see at once the absurdity of such a statement. He is an inventor, we will suppose, of this particular material, and has sold his patent to manufacture this material in Germany, we will say, and it is sold on liie market in Germany. Now, is there any private agreement that one could make with a German manufacturer that would prevent the person who bought this material in Germany from importing it into Canada ?
Certainly there is.
It is absurd to talk so.
The hon. minister does not know the ordinary conditions of trade, and I will illustrate that in a moment.
Will the hon. gentleman say that the goods manufactured in Germany cannot come in here ?

If a man has a patent to manufacture goods in Canada and the same patent is sold in England, the condition of the patent is thht the goods made in Canada cannot be sold in England, and the condition in the patent is that English goods shall not be sold in Canada, without any question. Now, let me show how close these trade arrangements are made. Let me give an illustration. If you go to an agent in London of French wines-I make this illustration, because it is something that happened to myself mot long ago-you buy from the French house in London so many cases of claret, or whatever it may toe, to he sold and sent to Canada at the price there. The house will simply say, when you tell them to send It to you in Canada :	We cannot do it, we
have an agent in Canada who has the sole control of the right of selling it there. I may buy it in London, true from the agent and ship it myself out here as an individual, but I cannot go into the market there and buy it through an agent to be sent to this country. That is an illustration in a small way, and a patent carries exactly the same conditions, only much more strictly. If a patent for acetylene gas or' carbide is sold in Canada and the patent is also sold in England and English goods are sent into Canada, the transaction will be attacked almost at once, and there will be a dispute Mr. OSLER.
straight and square between the manufacturer in England and the manufacturer in Canada.
That is a theory.
That is the practice.

We are not dealing in practice, we are dealing in carbides. Take this case. Assume that this patentee has sold his patent in other parts of the world-and I am sure that must be the case, because it is a useful article, and he would protect himself by getting this article patented. I think we may fairly assume that an article of this utility is being manufactured In all the civilized nations of the world, and the product of this patent is on the market. Suppose the hon. gentleman's theory is correct, and that the manufacturers in Canada should seek to put up the price, will he say what is to prevent the Canadian government, if they want to buy ten tons or any other quantity of this stuff, from going to the country where it is sold, say to Germany, and buying it there ? What is to prevent that, if it is for sale there ?

I am not a lawyer, and am not familiar with the Patent Act in theory, but I am familiar with the practice, and I know that the Patent Act protects the manufacturer in every country where that patent is running.

Does the hon. gentleman say there is anything in the patent laws of Canada that will prevent an article that is manufactured under a patent in some foreign country from being sold to a purchaser there and being taken into Canada ? Is there anything in our patent law to that effect ?

If the article is manufactured in England under the patent law and is sent here, at once the manufacturer in England will be notified that he cannot send that article out here. That Is always the case, and that practice is enforced as a matter of fact. I am not speaking of the law, but I am saying that, as a matter of fact, that is absolutely the case, the same as the copyright of a book. There is no question about it. If that were not so, what would be the use of selling the patent in England, or Germany, or France ? A patent iE England means that the patentee in England who manufactures cannot have the Canadian market; the patent in France means that the manufacturer in France can have nothing but the French market. However it may be in theory, in practice the patent in a country protects the manufacturer in that country. If that was not the case, what would be the use of our giving patents here to anybody ? It would not be worth while.	'	-

The patent might prevent buying and selling in this

*country, but this is not a question of importing. I think an article that is sojd in Europe, although it may be patented in Canada, could be brought into Canada. If a man chose to buy it in Europe he could bring it into Cana'da. If he chose to buy an article in a foreign country that is also the subject of a patent in Canada, I do not think there is anything in the customs law that will prevent him bringing that article into Canada.

The hon. gentleman is a lawyer and I ami not. Let one put this question to him. This carbide is patenteed in England, it is manufactured in England under the English patent. Can I, as a consumer of carbide, import from England all the carbide I want straight from the manufacturer in England, in defiance of the Canadian patent ? Will the minister answer that question ?
The hon. gentleman was making the statement that there was a monopoly, and I was asking him if he could tell me what the patent law was.
No, I do not know the patent law.

Then he is pretty much in the same position as myself. I would be very much surprised if when an article is manufactured in a foreign country and when a man has bought it and owns it, the patent law would prevent him from bringing it into this country. I could understand the patent law preventing a man from dealing in a patented article. I am merely theorizing the Act before him.

If the hon. Postmaster General were familiar with the Patent Act he would be aware that it forbids the use of any patented article in this country without the consent of the owner of the patent. If it were not so the patent would be practically useless.

I would like to give the committee a little illustration of this matter. The General Electric Company in the United States manufacture electrical goods for which they have the patents in the United States, and for which they have the patents in this country also. They are manufactured here by the Canadian General Electric Company. The Canadian General Electric Company manufacture these goods here and nobody else has the right to manufacture them. I want, for instance, to buy a certain kind of electrical motor that is manufactured by the Canadian General Electric Company. I think they are charging me too much for it. I write to the General Electric Company in the. United States and I ask them what they want for a ten horse power * electric motor. They write back that they
cannot sell one of these motors because they are made in Canada. All I have to do is to write over to my agent on the other side and tell him I want a ten horse power motor manufactured by the General Electric Company in the United States. He gets a price over there writes to me and I tell him to ship the motor at that price. I get the motor and we are doing it every day. The same thing applies to electric "lamps and other electrical goods.
Is it the same company i1

Certainly. We get the motor manufactured by the General Electric Company of the United States and we do so notwithstanding the fact that the article is patented and made by the Canadian General Electric Company.

Suppose they patented that in Canada and the United States and sold the right to manufacture in the United States ; the hon. gentleman gets his agent to send him over one of these articles on which there is a patent here. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say he can bring that article in here 1
I am speaking about goods patented here and patented there by the General Electric Company. If I want it I get my agent to get it for me.

I have the Patent Act under my hand, and I will read section 37 :
Every patent granted, under this Act, shall be subject and be expressed to be subject to the condition that such patent and all the rights and privileges thereby granted shall cease and determine, and that the patent shall be null and void at the end of two years from the date thereof, unless the patentee or his legal representatives, within that period, commence, and, after such commencement, continuously carry on in Canada the construction or manufacture of the invention patented, in such manner that any person desiring to use it may obtain it, or cause it to be made for him, at a reasonable price, at some manufactory or establishment for making or constructing it in Canada-and that such patent shall be void

This particular section has been amended, but not in the essential parts as regards this discussion.
-[DOT]if, after the expiration of twelve months from the granting thereof, the patentee or his legal representatives-
That is sthe agent which my hon. friend (Mr. Wright) was speaking of.
-or his assignees for the whole or in part of his interest in the patent imports or causes to be imported into Canada, the invention for which the patent is granted.
That is the law, so that in the case which my hon. friend has just spoken of the patent would be voided.
I do not care whether the patent is voided or not, I know we do it every day.

I did not intend to get into any controversy with the hon. Postmaster Genera] beeause he is a legal man and supposed to be familiar with the patent law, in theory, while I am only speaking of what I know from practice. The production of carbide is more or less of a monopoly, it is patented. The government have decided apparently to change the system of lighting the harbours and on their buoys. Now, do not for a moment think that I am objecting to that, because, as far as I know, acetylene gas has probably come to stay, and it is going to be a very advanced method of lighting as against what we have had. But, I say that before this government go into such an expenditure, before they make such a change, casting aside their old lighting apparatus and adopting a system of lighting which depends upon patents controlled by a small number of people, they ought to have an understanding with the manufacturers of this article that they shall have the right for a certain number of years, and a long number of years, to buy their product at a price not higher than that at which it is sold to anybody else in the market. I understand from the hon minister that no such arrangement has been made.

We do not intend to make such an arrangement.
Mr. OSLER, I do not wonder at that, I would not expect that the minister would intend to do it. The position we are adopting on this side of the House is that we have the right to criticise the transactions of the hon. minister. I think I am criticising the course of the hon. minister in regard to this matter quite fairly. I am not criticising the action which the hon. minister has taken in changing the system of lighting, because as far as I know, without knowing anything technical or scientific about the question, I understand that the lights are going to be better than the old lights that have been in use before. But, I say that the hon. minister, before he adopts that change, involving a large amount of money and committing the government practically for all time to come, or at all events until a new light is discovered, to the use of this material, the hon. minister should have an agreement with the men who have a monopoly of this material which is necessary to the government for a series of years providing that they will supply this material at as low a price as it is supplied to any person else.

From the argument of the hon. gentleman I would draw the inference that he is interested in get-Mr. CASGRAIN.
ting us to make a contract at $65 a ton with this company irrespective of whether the price may go down to $50 or $25 a ton within the next year or six months.

I think the last statement I made was that I suggested that the government should at all events make a contract with the company that they should be supplied with this material at the lowest price at which it is supplied in future to other people.
What do you want better than to buy it at the market price ? If these gentlemen in Ottawa are not disposed to sell us carbide at a reasonable price, we can buy it elsewhere.
You cannot buy it elsewhere. Nobody else makes it.
No.
Is it because we do not make a contract with them that they will not charge us more ? Do you think these people are fools ?

No.
Mi-. PREFONTAINE. Do you think they would sign any such contract? Of course the hon. gentleman wants to find fault, and I don't blame him ; perhaps I would no the same thing if I were in his position. But let us find fault within the bounds of reason, and not in connection with such a matter as this where there is no room for fault finding. We are not hound to buy from that particular company.
What other companies are manufacturing this article ?
The Willson Carbide Company of St. Catharines, and the Ottawa Carbide Company.

speechtext:
No.

531S

Yes, I know what I am talking about. There is a company authorized to start at Grand Falls; there is another that will be started at Shawinigan within a few months, and if there is any money in the business I suppose others will be organized. We are not paying an extreme price ; the fact is that we are just as businesslike as the Canadian Pacific Railway people.
I resent that assertion on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway would be bankrupt before the end of the year if they were not more businesslike than the minister.
They are paying the same,price as we are, $05 a ton, and they are buying a thousand tons where we buy twenty-five tons.
Does the minister buy all his carbide at $65 a ton ?
Yes.
How is it that the Auditor General reports that you pay $20 for 400 pounds ? What is the explanation of that ?
I have no answer to give.
In other words you have given that much boodle.
Boodle is in the mouth of the one who speaks about it.

The Auditor General's Report distinctly says that you bought 400 pounds of carbide for $20, and notwithstanding that the minister may throw back abuse, I can tell him that I prefer the Auditor General's record to his. If the Auditor General is right, an explanation is required of the minister.

I have the Patent Act before me now. Clause 44 says:
The government of Canada may at any time use any patent invention, paying to the patentee such sum as the commissioner reports to be reasonable compensation for the use thereof.
The definition of ' patent invention,' extends not only to the article itself but to the product of the article. It says :
The expression * invention ' means any new and useful art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter ; or any new and useful improvement in any art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.
It means not only the design but the product of the design, that if the owner of this patent had a monopoly, the government would have the right to ignore tho patent and fix a reasonable price.
I don't think there is any doubt about that. The government have the right to bring in auyAing free of duty, but that is not what we were talking about.

You were talking about how the government could be cornered. If the owners of this patent should seek an unfair price from the government the government could get its supply elsewhere and the patent does not restrain the government.
We do not suppose that the government would do an injustice to any patentee.
Nor would it do an injustice to the people of Canada.
I do not think you can find one single case where a patent owner in one country would undersell the man who holds the same patent in another country.

The hon. gentleman began his argument by saying that these people had a monopoly, and that they could compel the government to pay more than a reasonable price for the article. That contention could only hold if the Canadian patent prevented the government importing that article or if the patent were binding against the government. The patent law does not bind the government, and the monopoly argument falls to the ground.
I didn't talk about the government. I talked about the general principle.
The hon. gentleman talked about the supplying of carbide to the government.
Quite right; but I didn't suppose the answer would be that the government would take that position.
Oh. *

You need not laugh. I was not familiar with the Patent Act, but my statements are absolutely correct; more correct than the minister who answered me, although he is a lawyer I think ; I am in the judgment of the House on that point. I say further that if a patent owner in England were asked to sell to the Canadian government to the detriment of the man who owned the patent in Canada, the government would find that there existed a loyalty between the owners of patents in all countries which would prevent the request of the government being acceded to.

The hon. gentleman says there is a monopoly, but the question is whether these lighthouses can be



supplied with carbide without the government being compelled to pay an excessive price. %
Quite so.
Well, when the law says that the government may fix the price, how can the government be compelled to pay an excessive price ?

If the government are going to fix the price, they at once interfere with trade. The government have the right, I admit, but I do not think that that is an element which can enter into an argument of this sort. The government have the right to repudiate: their indebtedness to! their bondholders
How does the question of repudiation come in here ?

I admit that the government could at once take away the duties and admit the carbide free or give a bonus to an English manufacturer to compete with the Canadian, but allowing all that, I say that if the patent is held in Canada, England, France and Germany, all these companies will stand loyally together and prevent the government from breaking down the Canadian patent by buying cheaper elsewhere.

The hon. gentleman is straining hard for an argument when he advances one of that kind. He talks about repudiation, but if it is expressly stated in the Patent Act that the patent does not bind the Crown, how can there be any repudiation ? Should the owner of the patent endeavour to exact an unfair price, surely there can be nothing dishonourable in the government taking advantage of one of the conditions on which the patent is issued in order to protect the Canadian people.

The argument, in the first instance, was that if a man held a Canadian patent, you could bring him to terms by importing into Canada the articles for which hg holds.a patent, but that can only be done under certain conditions. According to section 7 of the amended Act of last session if any -holder of a patent who asks an unreasonable sum for the article he has patented, the government may grant a license to another party to manufacture the same article. If I want to buy an article and I can show that the holder of the patent is asking an unreasonable price, I can appeal to the department for a license to enable me to manufacture the article myself. Take the hon. gentleman's own department. A man takes out a patent for a mail bag and lock in Canada and the United States, so long as he sells at a reasonable figure, he is protected, and you cannot import these from the United States in violation of his patent.
Except as against the Crown.
Against any person so long as he does not charge an unreasonable price.

-We have a lighthouse at Summerside harbour, and I would like to know if this acetylene light is to be used there. If so, I would suggest that the substructure of the lighthouse should be repaired before putting in these expensive lights. I called attention a few days ago to this. The department should see that the Summerside lighthouse is put in proper repair and also the breakwater. I noticed the other evening, when the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) was asking why the ' Stanley ' was taken off the Sum-inerside and Cape Tormentine route, the reply was that the quantity of ice there made it too dangerous to leave the boat on that route. I take issue with the hon. gentleman. Where the hon. minister got his information I do not know, but I can only tell him that the ice, when the ' Stanley ' was taken away in December last, was no impediment whatever. The ' Stanley ' left on a very fine day. It took five hours to cross, which was an unusually long time with the conditions of the weather and the ice conditions in the harbour. In the meantime, during the whole fine day, with no notice or warning to any of the merchants or shippers of Prince Edward Island, without a word to those shipping their goods from the mainland to Prince Edward Island via Cape Tormentine, the boat left Cape Tormentine in the afternoon for Georgetown. They did not even wire to the shippers at Summerside until after the boat had left. In the meantime, the shippers at Summerside were hauling their freight, grain and products of one kind and another down to Summerside wharf to be shipped. It was not only an insult to the commercial interests of Prince Edward Island, but it was a wholly uncalled for act on the part of the department and their agents and Captain Brown upon whom * they were, apparently, depending to take the boat away from Summerside when we had absolutely fine weather and the ice conditions were favourable. Let me tell the committee something about the ice conditions. On the 28th December, 1903, there were six miles of ice, that had caught with the frost of practically the last night or two. In the heaviest part of it this ice was only two inches thick. We know the capacity of the ' Stanley.'

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) will allow me, we are not on the item of which he is speaking. I raise the question of order, Mr. Chairmin, We are on gas at the present time,, while the hon. gentleman is speaking about ice,; I think he is out of order.

I gathered from the acrimonious discussion that has gone on

that the whole field of the hon. gentleman's department was open for discussion.
Not at all.
And we have even gone beyond the department and have been discussing the Patent Law.
That applied to gas.

Well, I am going to try to get the minister to light these steamers with acetylene. Perhaps it will help to break the ice. This is a matter of interest to the committee and to the minister's department. The discussion of the subject has been opened and I think nothing will be gained by trying to rule me out of order. For, this is a matter that will be discussed.
^1 rise to a question of order. If we are here to stay all night, at least we should follow the rules.

I submit that I introduced this subject on the Summerside lighthouse, and I am now moving toward the Cape Tormentine light ; and I want to get the track clear of ice. As I said, the steamer passing out from the Summerside lighthouse with only two inches of ice backed up some twenty odd times. She got out of the harbour very easily but took a much longer time than she usually takes. She got down off Cape Tormentine lighthouse in about five hours. As I said, the conditions were as favourable for the boat continuing this service as at any time during the year, and the department are certainly to blame for allowing her to be taken away.. Now, I turn to the report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and I find here a letter from the deputy minister on the island service. I must say I take issue with the explanations of the Deputy Minister. I think I know as much about the conditions there as the Deputy Minister does, and I submit that the report is, to a large extent not correct, but conveys a wrong impression as to the situation in regard to the winter, service. The minister told us last session that he was going down to Prince Edward Island to look over the service, and he| did go down.

I rise to a question of order. The item under discussion is * salaries and allowances to lighthouse keepers,' and with this the question of the service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland has nothing to do. If we are going to stay all night we will stay all night, but we might as well follow the rules. If the hon. gentleman was not here last night to discuss the question when the item under which it would properly arise was before the committee, he can take some other opportunity to discuss it.
169J

I think the hon. member (Mr. Lefurgey) is wandering a little from the question before the chair. He is an old member of the House and knows the importance of carrying on the debate in an orderly way. The item before us is salaries and allowances of lighthouse keepers, and, under that item I think he can hardly discuss the question to which he has been referring.

Then, how was the discussion allowed to go on for two hours on acetylene gas and patents '? The question I have to bring before the committee is of great Importance to the people of my section-of more importance than the subject that the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) and some other gentlemen have been discussing for so long, a discus-, sion with absolutely no point or purpose. Now, I have a point and purpose ixi this,' and it is to show up the mismanagement-
I must call the hon. member (Mr. Lefurgey) to order. I think I can hardly allow this discussion. I must ask him to keep to the question under consideration.

I understand, Mr. Chairman, that you rule my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) out of order. I beg to move that the committee rise.
Mr- FIELDING. There will be no difficulty in finding ample opportunity to discussing the question to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) has referred. It is an important question, but it does not happen to be related to the subject before the chair. Hon. members on both sides are interested in seeing that we confine ourselves within a reasonable regard for the rules. This is not a party question at all.' We can keep one another here many months if we depart from the rules and allow too wide a range of discussion. I would appeal to my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) not to insist upon a division upon the question, but to observe the ruling of the chair. Another opportunity will be afforded for discussing the question which has been referred to the importance of which I recognize. '

I am well on with the discussion of the subject now, and I would like to finish what I have to say 1 do not intend to occupy more than a few minutes, and I would like to finish and get -m ex-' planation from the minister.

(Mr. Campbell). Mr. the committee rise.

I hope mV hon. friend from Prince will accept the suggestion I offer. The motion is quite in order, of course, but I appeal to the hon. gentleman to assist us in conducting the business of the House and not to ask a division on such

I am anxious to expedite the business of the House and get through the session. But. I find an effort being made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to shut off my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) in the discussion of the subject he has brought before the committee. I would ask, in the interest of all concerned, that the hon. member for East Prince be allowed to make his statement. .

On the very next item we take up 'Agencies, rents and contingencies ' it would be perfectly in order for my hon. friend to make the remarks that he was addressing to the House; but on this particular item I do not think he can make them.

speechtext:
<
lapse of time. This year, the requirements of navigation demanded an additional month of service. We are always ready to ao all in our power to be of service to navigation, both early in the spring and late In the fall. To do so it is necessary to keep a complete crew, and a greater amount of provisions, which costs a large amount.
We, therefore, beg of you to allow us an additional month of salary, pro rata, In order to indemnify us for such expenditure and for the services that we rendered. We also desire to draw your attention to the fact that early in the springtime navigation work is cold and hard ; and in the fall it is not only cold and hard but also dangerous. Hoping that you will take our petition into favourable consideration, we have the honour to be your very humble servants.
Keeper of lie Rouge floating lighthouse. '

CAPT. ESDKAS LEBEL, [DOT]
Keeper of Bas de la Traverse floating lighthouse.
(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the salaries are being' increased everywhere on the ground that the cost of living is higher and these men are forced to work one month more without getting more pay. Out of the $2,400 which are granted, the captain must provide for a mate, an engineer, and pay the crew and hoard them. Just think of the amount remaining to the captain after all those expenses have been paid. I hope the hon. minister will he able to take from these $238,000 the amount required to comply with the request of these three gentlemen, since we want them to remain at work for a longer time in view of improving the navigation in the lower St. Lawrence.

(Translation.) Of course, I will consider the request made by my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Gau-vreau) if the facts stated by him are true, that is, if these gentlemen are obliged to work fifteen days longer in spring and fifteen days longer in fall, it appears to me that their petition for an increase is only fair and reasonable. Although this estimate does not amount to so large a sum as that of last year, yet I may assure my hon. friend that steps will be taken in order that justice be done to whom justice is due, and I think the men he has mentioned are entitled to that, if he has stated the facts correctly.

Does this apply only to these three men mentioned by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) ? I think the same principle should apply to all those who, under the new regulations, have to be in the lighthouses 15 days earlier in the spring and 15 days later in the fall.

(Translation.) It goes without saying that the same principle must be applied everywhere. It is hut reasonable that he who is hound to work

for a longer time whether it be at Kamou-raska or at Temiseouata, should get more pay. The principle is fair and resonable in every case. If you force an employee to work during a longer time than he was obliged to when he took service, I think it but fair that you should pay him more on account of those additional services.

I think the hon. gentleman is perfectly right. But under the circumstances he should increase this vote of $238,000. He will never be able to pay the same salaries he is paying now, and he will never be able to increase the salaries, as he says he contemplates doing, unless he increases this vote.

(Translation.) Before the supplementary estimates for next year are brought down I will have time to consider this question, and I say again that I will endeavour to do justice to whom justice is due.
(Translation.) I was just going to ask the hon. minister if he could not have the necessary amount voted in the supplementary estimates.
I understood the minister to say that he had dispensed with several light keepers on adopting the new system. How many did he dispense with ?
I read the statement about an hour ago and will read it again if the hon. gentleman desires. We dispensed with four.
So all the change the hon. gentleman has made amounts to dispensing with the services of four light keepers.
So far.
These are marvellous changes.
There are other marvellous changes.

The minister stated that when this new system was introduced there would be a great saving in maintenance of the lights, he said there would be a saving of $10,500 a year. Does he expect that saving to take place in the near future ?
I stated that the saving for the present would be $1,610 a year.

I will read what the hon. gentleman said last year when he was giving to the committee the reasons for changing the old system of lighting to the new system :
The ten new ranges of gas lights will require no keepers, saving an annual charge of $3,000, and the proposed conversion of the lights from an oil to a gas basis will enable the keepers to be dispensed with as opportunity offers, at a saving of $7,000 per year, or a total saving in cost of maintenance of $10,500 per year.
What has the hon. gentleman to say to that ?

Last year I spoke of the installation of the new lights according to a new system. Of course that cannot all be done in one year. We cannot get the apparatus as fast as we would like to make the change. Last year we could only make the change in respect to four lights. We could not go faster profitably, but some hon. gentlemen opposite think we have gone too fast. We think we have been acting in the best interests of the department. Of course there are other lights besides these four where the new system will be installed.
In what places are the lights now in operation ?
For the present we have'only made these four changes, which are on the upper lakes.

There was a statement made some two or three years ago. perhaps not . by the hon. gentleman, but by his predecessor that there would be some changes in respect to the insurance rates on the St. Lawrence route when this new system was installed. Can the hon. gentleman make a statement in regard to that matter :

1 think I gave some information in regard to this question at the beginning of the session when I stated that I had been informed by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that they had obtained for their boats a special reduction in the insurance rates. I am sorry that I cannot boast, and I think every business man in this country will share my regret, that we have not yet obtained a general reduction. It is a matter which takes a long time to settle but I think that everybody should join hands in trying to better the conditions of the St. Lawrence route. We have been trying to do that and I do not think that any fault can be found with what has been done, at least since I have been at the head of the department. I have put myself at the disposal of the shipping interests, and of the Boards of Trade of different places and I have tried to carry out their recommendations. It will take some time yet but when we have carried out all the improvements and alterations that are contemplated, if we do not obtain from the British insurance companies a reduction in rates, it will be time for us to make a move so as to force the insurance companies to recognize the sacrifices that have been made by the' Canadian government in order to improve the route. I think that at the present moment I can boast of the fact that we have not been reproached bv any Board of Trade or any shipping federation that we have not tried to do what was best to improve the route of the St. Lawrence. Any suggestion that hon. gentlemen are disposed to give the department

will certainly be received with the greatest consideration and we will try to do the best under the circumstances.

In reference to the remarks which the hon. minister has just made as to insurance rates, I quite agree with him that nothing can be done except on business principles. I am not sure that I can agree with him that all that can be done has been done because I think that the improvement of the St. Lawrence, the proper lighting and development of the route, is of far greater importance to Canada than any transcontinental railway or any other work that is contemplated or suggested, and I do not think that the government are devoting half enough of their energy to the development of that route. This is the one way of spending money that will receive the endorsement of every man in Canada. Going back to our discussion in regard to acetylene gas I would like to ask the hon. minister who is the officer in charge of the work of replacing the old lighting with the new lights and under what recommendation the hon. minister is acting.
The engineers and staff of the department.
Who is the head man ?

The chief engineer of the department is Col. Anderson, but since last winter I have thought proper to organize a special lighthouse board composed of a number of my officials with power to call in representatives of the marine interests. When a question which interests one section of the country is to be considered these outside gentlemen will be called in. At the same time I thought it proper to appoint a special officer as lighthouse commissioner, Mr. J. F. Fraser who was employed in the department before I took charge of it. This gentleman was acting under the supervision and control of the head of the department. He has certain special duties to perform while at the same time the chief engineer remains with certain duties to perform. We felt in doing so that we were serving the interests of navigation and transportation and that we were trying to satisfy the general public interest especially in navigation because representatives of these interests would have an opportunity to be heard before this board, to make their representations and to present arguments. This board was instituted about five months ago. As far as I can learn from people interested in navigation it has given entire satisfaction. Questions that have been pending as regards the establishment of lights at certain points and about which there have been differences of opinion have been decided, and decided favourably to the interests of navigation. I think in acting in that way we have done what is best in the interest of the'country.
