speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman a report from the gentleman he named, Col. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
Anderson, in reference to this change from the old method to the new ?
I do not know what the gist of the hon. gentleman's question is.

The hon. minister says that Col. Anderson is in charge of the work connected with this proposed change of lighting from the old system to the new and I want to know if he has a report from that officer.

There is no proposed change. The change was made four or five months ago and Col. Anderson is a member of the board. He has never refused to act on the board and I do not know that he has offered any objection to the decisions or deliberations of the board.
That is not the question I asked. I asked whether there was a report from this gentleman to the department in any shape or form in connection with the change of lighting.
None whatever.
No report, confidential or otherwise ?
None whatever.
May I ask the hon. minister who Mr. Fraser is, when he was appointed to the department and if he had been formerly in any shape or way connected with an acetylene gas company i

Fraser was appointed in 1893. He is a graduate of the Royal Military College and he was employed in the department on the staff of the chief engineer. He was considered the most suitable person to occupy that position of lighthouse commissioner.
He has been in the employ of the government ever since ?
Since 1893.
Did you declare that item carried, Mr. Chairman, when I had a motion before the chair that the committee rise ?
I understood the hon. member had withdrawn the motion.

I did not withdraw. I am required to give a reason why this committee should rise, and my reason is that my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Le-furgey) was endeavouring to show that the terms of confederation with Prince Edward Island have not been carried out, and he was refused a hearing by the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Finance, and in justice to the hon. member (Mr. Lefurgey)
I make this motion in order that he may be heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The statement that the hon. member (Mr. Lefurgey) was refused a

hearing by the Minister of Finance is erroneous. All I suggested was that the hon. gentleman should wait until the question was properly before the House. I quite agree that the question is an important one, but even important questions have their proper place.
The hon. gentleman for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) has given the House just cause why this question should be discussed at the present time.

On a motion that the committee rise, you can only discuss the question as to why the committee should rise, and it is not proper to discuss a question relating to transportation in Prince Edward Island.

That is just exactly what I am going to do. The chairman must know that the government has not carried out the terms of confederation with Prince Edward Island, and that is the question which I am discussing at present.
I am quite sure that the hon. member wishes to facilitate the business of the House, and I would point out to him that on the very next item he can discuss this question.

The reason why the committee should rise is that the government are not carrying out the terms of confederation with Prince Edward Island. Wo are not satisfied with the efforts nor with the bona fides of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and we say that justice is not done to Prince Edward Island.
I call the hon. gentleman to order. We are now considering the vote for salaries and allowances to lighthouse keepers.
The motion is that the committee shall rise-
Question.
I wish to speak on this question of order which has been raised by the Minister of Marine. If this kind of thing goes on any longer my hon. friend will not get very far in his estimates.
Oh ; bluff.

I say that on a motion that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, hon. members can not only discuss the question as to why the committee should rise, but they can go on with the discussion as on a motion to adjourn the House. I tell my hon. friends on the other side that they will not advance their business by trying to cry us down.
Whajt difference does it make anyway ?
Question.

I am speaking to the question, and so long as my hon. friends go
on in that way the business of the House will not be advanced.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not justified in using the threat that such and such will take place.

I am not using any threat, but I am asking you, as chairman, to maintain order ; and I say that those gentlemen who are trying to cry me down are not in order. It is your duty to ask them to keep order, and not to call me to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I beg the hon; gentleman's pardon if I have done anything wrong. When an hon. member is interrupted, he himself has the right to complain, but as some hon. gentlemen like to be interrupted, if the Speaker interferes-
How is it you interfered and called me to order when no hon. member complained ?	*
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want the hon. gentleman to understand that no hon. gentleman has the right to throw out the threat that such and such a thing will take place unless he has his way. That is a well known rule.

I rise to speak on the point of order. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) was giving reasons why the committee should rise, and he associated with those reasons the urgent demands of Prince Edward Island, and he can talk to the committee until to-morrow morning if he likes and be quit? within the rules of the House.
iSome hon. MEMBERS. Go on.
So long as the hon. gentleman keeps within the rules of debate and the rules of the House, he can talk as long as he likes on that question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman please tell me what the point of order is ? It was raised before I came m.
The point of order, as T understand it, is as to what the hon. gentleman had a right to talk to on the motion that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: iSurely my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule), on a moment's reflection, will not take the ground he practically does-that on a motion that the committee rise an hon. member may talk on any subject under heaven.
I made no such statement, and I want to tell the hon. Minister of Finance that there is not a man with a spark of manhood in him would misrepresent me as he has done.
Oh, oh.

He knows I made no such statement. I said he could talk on

the subject before the House, the motion that was made before the House, and give any reasons that he desired to give to the House ; not that he could talk on any subject but talk on that one subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point which we raise is that the hon. member in making the motion must confine himself to reasons connected with the subject under consideration.
That is what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, he said the hon. member was quite at liberty to introduce other matters and give anv reasons he pleased.
I deny it, and the minister has no right to state it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just at present I have the right to b* on the floor; my hon. friend has not.
He has not the right to misrepresent me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must withdraw that remark, that I misrepresented him ; that is not parliamentary.

I say deliberately, if you make that statement, you misrepresent me, and I repeat it.
Mr. JiTELDING. I do not want any words about it, but if my hon. friend wants to quarrel I demand that he withdraw these words.
I shall not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this hon. gentleman-I regret it because he and I have generally got on very well-I want to ask if he adheres to the statement that I de-! liberately misrepresented him.
I did not say deliberately. I said he had not the right to misrepresent me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman inserted the word deliberately.
Yes, he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: ' Hansard ' will show the hon. gentleman used the word deliberately.
No, I said, ' I say deliberately that the hon. gentleman misrepresented me,' and I meant it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not going to quarrel with my hon. friend on that but I have raised a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An hon. member has not the right to say that another hon. member has deliberately misrepresented him.
If you were listening to me you must understand that I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point on which I want a ruling is whether an hon. member on making a motion to rise, should confine himself to reasons connected with the subject before the House, or whether he is at liberty to introduce new matter.

I am reading now from Bourinot, page 523 :
It is not regular to move an adjournment of the debate on a question or an adjournment of the sittings of the committee to a future time ; but certain motions may be made with the same effect. If it is proposed to defer the discussion of a Bill or resolution, the motion may be made-' That the chairman do report progress and ask leave to sit again ' ; and if this motion (which is equivalent to a motion for the adjournment of the debate) be agreed to, the committee rises at once, and the chairman reports accordingly.
I call your attention to the statement which is made here in Bourinot that the motion that the Chairman of the committee report progress and ask the committee to sit again is equivalent to a motion for the adjournment of the debate. Now there is no ruling better known than that on a motion for the adjournment of a debate, the; House is not at all limited to the question which is then being discussed by the House, because then there would be no cause to; make a motion for the adjournment of the debate. When the motion that the committee rise, is made, I take it that you can then discuss what you could discuss on the motion that the debate be adjourned. The motion that the debate be adjourned is made in order that a member may bring in another subject than the subject which is being debated when the motion is made. My hon. friend says : ' For one reason or another I was not able to discuss the ques-f tion which came up yesterday and which is not now before the House. However I move that the committee do rise now, and report progress and ask leave to sit again. For what reason ? In order that I may bel able to discuss this question which was discussed yesterday ;* not to discuss the particular question in debate when this motion was made.' If my hon. friend will say to the House that the reason for which " he makes this motion is to discuss the most important question which he is about to discuss he will be perfectly in order. He has brought before the House an important question and the reason for which he asked that the committee rise, was because he wants to discuss that question. It seems to me that if you only give me one of your ears, Mr. Chairman, I will be able to convince you that the Finance Minister is not quite right and that Bourinot is against him on this point.

-Mr. FIELDING. If Bourinot is against me, my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) has neglected to point out the passage. He has quoted nothing against me. I accept my hon. friend's own statement that the hon. gentleman moves that the committee rise in order that he may have an opportunity of discussing a question which was properly before the committee yesterday. In that view members could constantly be taking up matters already dealt with, and my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) is too good a constitutional lawyer to believe anything of the sort.
I understood my hon. friend to advise him to withdraw the motion although it was perfectly in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite admit that the motion is in order, but I do not admit that another hon. gentleman had the right to make a speech on another subject in connection with the motion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not see that we are saving much time. The hon. member from Prince Edward Island said it would take him only about ten minutes to conclude and then we could proceed with the next item. Let him conclude and then let us proceed. I think it will be better in the interests of peace, harmony and good-will to allow the hon. gentleman to proceed and have his remarks all together.
To have peace and harmony we had better follow the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We must bear in mind one or two points in considering this matter. There are two motions which can be made while in committee terminating the sitting of the committee. One is that I do leave the chair. That is equivalent to the adjournment of the House. There is another motion which is that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again. That is equivalent to the adjournment of the debate in the House. Now understanding these two points, let me read Bourinot :
Nor is it in order under cover of a motion for adjournment-to put a question which the Speaker has declared irregular, or when there is a question before the House and a member moves the adjournment, he must confine himself to the question.
That is my decision.
What question ?
The question before the House.
The question before the House, is the reason why I moved the committee rise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is a question very frequently put when it is meant that the chairman leave the chair it is put in this way : that the committee rise. But that is not a proper form. If you stop at' ' the committee rise ' it is equivalent to the
chairman leaving the chair. The other motion, which is equivalent to the adjournment of the debate in the House, is that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. That is an adjournment of the day's work. The motion that I leave the chair is equivalent to a motion of adjournment in the House.
Do I understand by your ruling that I am out of order ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question before the House is that I do leave the chair.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member be good enough to submit to the decision of the Chair or appeal against it ? The Chair has decided that he cannot discuss any other question hut the one he raised at the particular time when he raised it.

Am I to understand that after the motion that the committee rise and the statement of the hon. member for West Prince that it rises for a particular purpose to discuss a very important matter we cannot discuss that matter ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: You cannot introduce a new question.
I submit that this is not a new question.
Order.

We will then talk on acetylene gas. I submit that the lighthouse in Summerside harbour should be supplied with this light and that the minister should instruct his deputy to pay more attention to the general repairs and conduct of' the lighthouse service around Prince Edward Island. The largest portion of the traffic of Prince Edward Island comes in and goes out of the harbour at Summerside, and we trust that a winter mail service will be established at that point and carried on without the humbugging which characterized it during the past winter. I would like to impress upon the minister the necessity of having an arrangement concluded before next winter comes on, so that the boats will be in possession of every facility for the resumption of this service.
Motion negatived

I brought up last week the question of buoying the Napanee river and was promised the information I asked for. I did not get it until after the House took recess at six o'clock, but I find that the fault is not with the contractor. When I was at home a few days ago, he pointed out to me the difficulty. He had a letter from the department dated the 17th of April, 1903, authorizing him to go on putting out the buoys in the season of 1903 and informing him that a contract would be sent for him to sign. He went on and did the work as instructed. On the 1st of July a contract was sent to him to be signed' for a year, and he Signed it believing that the department would do as it had done hitherto, and consider that when he put out the buoys in the spring and looked after them during the summer and took them in again in the fall, his years' work would be done. It appears however that the department want to hold him until the 1st of June of this year and instructed him to put out the buoys again this spring. He got a lawyer to write to the department but could not find out whether the department would pay him for the extra work of putting out the buoys this spring. He therefore refused to put them out and the department have called for tenders. It seems to me that the department is to blame. They had a servant who was faithfully discharging his duty and was not getting too much for the work he did and they should have continued him in that service.

The difficulty
seems to me to be that the contractor is disappointed because we have not given him the job. He got a contract for one year and fulfilled it, and now he wants it for three years more. The department decided to call for tenders. What objection has this man to tendering again ?

The difficulty is that the department want to hold him for a year from the time he signed the contract although he had done his year's work. Here is a letter written by Mr. Herrington to the department, dated May 23rd :
Dear Sir,-I handed your letter of the 19th instant to Mr. Mowers, and while your intention may he clear, yet your letter is capable of two constructions.
Mr. Mowers had earned one year's salary by putting out the buoys last year and taking them in again in the fall.
It is true that his contract was dated the 1st June, but it really should have been dated the 18th or 19th of April, as he did immediately upon the receipt of your letter of the 17th April, 1903, go to work and prepare and put out the buoys, whereas the contract in which this very work was done is dated the 1st June.
It is better to have a clear understanding in thfe beginning. He is prepared to go on and prepare the buoys and put them out this season, Mr. 'LEFURGEY.
but he would require some assurance that he will receive pay for this year's work.
If the ' Scout ' takes over his contract and takes them up next fall, what pay is he to receive for putting them out this spring, as his work of preparing and putting them out is fully five times as serious as the matter of taking them in 7 Mr. Mowers is not at all disposed to cavil over the matter, but as it was a mistake that the contract was ever dated the 1st June instead of the 18th or 19th of April, you can readily see that it is of the first importance to him that you and he should understand one another.
We presume that you do not contend that the pay he has already received is to cover the work you are now asking him to do.
If you will make this clear in a telegram to Mr. Mowers or to myself the work will be proceeded with.
It does seem to me that that is a very plain statement. All the minister or his deputy needed to do was to write a letter or send a telegram saying that Mr. Mowers would be paid. They write a letter and say that he will be paid, but call 'attention to the fact that the contract was for a year and the year was not up. So, he said : I will not do the work because I do not believe they will pay me. And what is the result ? Up to this hour the'river is not buoyed. Is that the way the public service is to be neglected ? And all because the hon. minister or his deputy would not write a letter saying that a man who did certain work would be paid for doing it. I think the minister ought to tell us the reason why he did not write such a letter.

I have explained the matter already a couple of times. And further discussion seems to me a loss of time. Mr. Mowers had a contract for a year to put out the buoys, and this contract expired on 1st of June. According to our interpretation of the contract, it was his duty to put out the buoys this season. He refused to do so and wanted a contract for three years. We wTould not consent, but have now decided to call for tenders. We did call for tenders and they will be in in a few days. Mr. Mowers is free to tender like the others. Because we would not consent to give him a contract for three years -blame is sought to be attached to us for his neglect to carry out his contract.

I wonder if the minister is more used to holding people up than to being held up. Here is the letter I referred to :
Ottawa, April 17th, 1903.
Sir,-I have to inform you that the department will enter into a contract with you for one year for maintaining the buoy service on the Napanee river for the sum of $60 per annum, the amount paid you formerly for this service.
I have to request you to forward the name of two sureties and a contract will be made out and sent you for signature. In the mean-

time you may have the buoys prepared and placed in position as soon as possible.
That is signed by the deputy minister. It does seem to me that when he put out the buoys in the spring, and took care of them in the summer and took them in in the fall he had honestly performed his contract.
If the hon. gentleman's friend is not satisfied, let him give it up or tender with the others.

I am not dealing with this as a question in which one person is interested. It is a question of the public service and the rights of the people in that section. The river is not buoyed as it ought to be.
The water is higher than it ever was, and nobody is suffering.

I would like to know if a vessel is not as likely to go aground in a narrow river when the water is high as when it is low. The water covers the marshes and shallows, and, unless the person in charge of the vessel knows the channel well I believe he is even more likely to run his boat aground when the water is high than when the water is low.
Have there been any accidents ?
I do not know, but the minister is not to get credit if there have not been.
The reports from my department show that there is no danger at the present time.
Then, why buoy the river if there is no danger ?
It will be buoyed in good time.
Under a contract for one year has the contractor to put the buoys out twice and take them in once ?
That is the interpretation we put on this contract having a contract expiring 1st of June he had to do the work twice.
Then, this is simply a misunderstanding with the holder of the contract.

That is exactly what I say. There is a misunderstanding on a question of $60. Why should the hon. gentleman raise such a cry and spend so much of the time of the House discussing such a question when this man has the privilege of tendering again ?
There is a very serious side to this question. If a man puts out the buoys in the spring and takes them in at the close of navigation he would perform one year's service.
We do not read it that way.

Surely there can be no question about it. The minister is taking advantage of mere technicality in the contract. The man says he is willing to put out the buoys a second time if he is paid, and surely he is entitled to be paid for the work he does.
Why did he not put them out in the spring like an honest man ? He would then have been entitled to $30, according to the hon. gentleman. But he did not do it ; he wanted to hold us up.
No, he was willing to put out the buoys a second time if the department would pay him.
Where do you find that ?

In the statement of the deputy which I have here :
I have to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of 13th instant in which you state that Mr. Blakely Mowers expects to be paid for placing the buoys next spring.
That is the statement of the hon. gentleman's own department.	.

Go on. Read.
Mr. INGRAM (reading)

It is not at all the intention of the department to ask Mr. Mowers to put out the buoys without paying him for them this year.

Go on. Read.
Mr. INGRAM (reading)

He entered into a contract nearly a year ago and it will terminate in June.
' It will terminate in June.'

Go on. Read.
Mr. INGRAM (reading)

The department has placed on the St. Lawrence river the steamer ' Scout ' and many changes have been made in the buoy service with the intention of performing the work with the department's steamer. It is expected to take over the work that is now under Mr. Mower's contract and have it done by the steamer ' Scout.'
Go on.
That is the end. This gentleman, in fulfilment of his contract, put out the buoys and afterwards took them in.
He has been paid.
He has done a season's work, has he not ? The department says his contract does not finish until 1st of June and he must put out the buoys a second time.
But he did not put them out. What complaint does he make ?

Here he is told that the work was to be taken over and done by

the steamer ' Scout.' Why not pay the man for putting out the buoys a second time ?
Because he did not put them out a second time.
Because you refused to pay him.
This man seems to have met with bad treatment. The minister asks what complaint he makes. Does the minister think he is bound to do a year and a half's work for a year's pay ?
No.

I listened carefully to the discussion, and I think I am right In saying that that is in effect what the department demanded. It seems that he put out the buoys and afterwards took them in and has been paid for a year's work. The department ought to be ashamed of trying to enforce this contract merely because it was dated on the 1st of June. I think this man was clearly entitled to be paid for his extra work, and the department ought to be ashamed, if it is possible for them to be ashamed of anything, for refusing to say they would pav him if he did it

The action of the minister in this matter I think deserves all the censure he is getting. But that is not the most important question. The minister apparently does not realize the fact that the government has undertaken the public duty of buoying this river. They have always done it at a certain date of the year, and the minister asks whether any accident has happened because that was not done. Suppose no buoys had been put on the St. Lawrence, and the government had saved $800 or $8,000 in consequence, and no accident had happened, would that be any excuse for the minister not having put in the buoys at the proper time ? The charge is serious enough for this individual, but, much more serious for the minister hfmself, in having allowed the river to remain unbuoyed to this late date of the season, and the boats to run the risk of accident.
My size is just as big as the hon. gentleman's.

I can tell the minister that he cannot bluff us. We have read about the hon. gentleman, and I can tell him that if he is going to indulge in crooked transactions of this character he is guilty of undignified conduct, and there is no language by which we can characterize it in terms of sufficient contempt. Then the hon. gentleman says :	Why, there has been no
accident. Suppose accidents had occurred, he would have been responsible for them. Can it be that this hon. gentleman has such an exalted idea of his business ability that he can permit himself to resort to miserable, contemptible tactics of this kind. If that is the hon. gentleman's estimate of the proper way of conducting his department, I can assure him he will not succeed very well. Before I had read this correspondence I thought the hon. gentleman must have had some reason, some excuse for refusing to pay this man, but since I have lead it I am bound to say that he has no excuse.

I may tell the hon. gentleman at once that his contempt does not reach the ankle of my foot. All I have to say about this matter is this : Mr. Mowers got a contract for putting buoys in the Napanee river.
When did the year commence ?

It commenced on June 1, 1903. I am ready to take the interpretation of the hon. gentleman of the mean-

mg of that contract. He got a contract for putting out the buoys for one year. Am I right in understanding that the interpretation put upon the contract by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) is that it expired at the time the buoys were taken in ? Is that the hon. gentleman's interpretation ?
Yes.
I will tell you when you get through.

Then I conclude that is the interpretation that he puts upon the contract. If the year, whenever it expired, meant $60 for the year, and meant putting in the buoys in the spring and taking them out in the fall he would be paid for one season's work, but he would have to continue the service until June 1, 1904, and be paid extra this spring. There is no use working up such contempt about so simple a matter. There is no use getting so excited about it. I am not at all excited over it. I do not cast personalities against any person in this House. I am perfectly free to do so, but I refrain because it would be undignified on my part. Now, suppose the contract meant what the hon. gentleman from Lennox pretends, that the buoys were to be, put in in the spring and taken up in the fall. The man's contract was from 1st June, 1903, to 1st June, 1904, and whatever work was necessary within that time he should have done. He was paid $60 for last year's work, and would have been paid $30 more if he had placed the buoys in the spring before June of this year. When spring came it seems that there was a misunderstanding, I admit that. Mr. Herrington-I am not saying that he interfered with the department-wanted this gentleman to get a contract for three years. We said : No, we do not intend to give a contract for three years, we intend to have this service done in another manner. What did it mean ? It meant that if Mr. Mowers had put back the buoys in the spring he would have been entitled to $30 for his actual work. The department never told him he would not be paid for his work. But, he was badly advised, and he said : No, I will not put them out unless I get a contract for three years. Mr. Mowers was an uneducated man, because he does not seem to know how to write, and he was advised by other parties not to do anything until he got his own way.
Will the hon. gentleman read from the correspondence the statement that he wanted a three year's contract?

The correspondence is in the department, but this is the information I get from my officers. He refused point blank to put the buoys out in the spring, but wanted a contract for three years. I do not know anything about this small potato matter, as it has been called by some hon. members on the other side of the House, and if he wanted to secure this $30 extra it would have been very easy for him to have put out the buoys, but he did not do it. We do not owe him anything, He tlid not spend anything). Tenders have been asked for this work and he can tender if he thinks proper. The great argument, however, is that these buoys have not been put out and that there might be danger to navigation. I have to rely on my officers as regards that. My officers report to me that there is no hurry to put the buoys out because the water is so high that there can be no danger at the present moment. It is all very well to argue like my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) who is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway that if you do not put buoys out in the St. Lawrence an accident may occur but in this case that argument cannot apply. We know perfectly well that in certain seasons of the year there can be scarcely any danger in leaving a small river without buoys. The fact of the matter is that not later than two days ago there were no buoys at all on Lake St. John which is an immense lake in the province of Quebec and we had to send an officer up there because the contractor had not put the buoys out. Things of this kind happen every day, but there was no danger there any more than there is in the Napanee river because the buoys are put out only to indicate shoal water. At the present moment the water is high enough and navigation can be carried on over the whole lake without any danger. There was no disposition on the part of the department to ill-use this contractor or take advantage of him in any way. If he had performed any work that he was not obliged to do under his contract he would have no reason to believe that the department would not have paid him.

I am a little bit surprised at the statements made by the hon. minister, and that accounts to me for the answers that he gave because he desired that they should be interpreted either way. The deputy minister wrote :
He entered into the contract nearly a year ago and it will terminate in June.
Notwithstanding that, the deputy minister had written him in April, 1903, urging him to go on and do the work and saying they would send the contract for him to sign. On the strength of that letter he got the buoys ready and put them in their places. Here is a copy of the receipt that Mr. Mowers signed for the pay for the work and the department at that time did consider
5343 '

that he had carried out his year's contract. Mr. Herrington told him that the letters that he was getting from the department were liable to be interpreted in two ways and Mr. Mowers wanted to get an understanding from the department as to the work which he was to do. In the face of that he failed to get any declaration from the department. The hon. minister does not seem to haye much confidence in Mr. Herrington.
I do not know him.

He is the leading Liberal in Lennox, a gentleman who goes out and stumps against me and we are just as good friends as the minister and I or a little better. Mr. Herrington is one of the strongest Liberals in that district and he is just as disagreeable on the stump as my hon. friend is in office. This gentleman has taken the pains to write for Mr. Mowers, and he himself puts this interpretation on the letters he gets. It would have been the easiest thing in the world for the hon. minister or for his deputy to direct that a telegram be sent to Mr. Herrington : Tell Mr. Mowers to do the work and we will pay him for it. I know of nothing in regard to a two or three years contract. As I can quite understand Mr. Mowers would prefer to have a contract for three years rather than for one year because sometimes the buoys get out of order and if he has to make a new one it would be better for him to have a three years' contract because the buoys last that long. In this case Mr. Mowers was prepared to go on and do the work if he had got an answer from the department.

It is perfectly plain that the hon. minister wanted to make us believe something which is not borne out by this correspondence. What was the object of the deputy minister in writing that Mr. Mowers' contract terminated on the first of June ? He wrote asking about putting the buoys out in the spring. It is all very well for the hon. minister to talk about entering into personalities in connection with a matter of this kind. I have not said anything personal against the hon. minister himself but I am condemning this transaction, but if it is personal to call it contemptible I will repeat that. I have nothing against the hon. gentleman personally nor against any other minister of the Crown but it does not follow that because I have that regard for him I am to sit here and endorse a transaction of this character. The hon. gentleman cannot read that correspondence and come to any other conclusion than that which I have come to in regard to it. What was the object of writing in this way, if it were not to take advantage of this man ? It requires no lawyer to interpret that; a layman can interpret the object of writing that letter.

It appears very plainly on the face of this correspondence, that the whole difficulty has arisen in the department, and that Mr. Mowers was perfectly justified in the position he took, that he should not do a year and a half's work for one year's pay. The letter of the 17th of April, 1903, makes that perfectly plain. The deputy minister writing to Mr. Mowers says :
I have to inform you that the department will enter into a contract with you for one year.
That was not one year from June, 1903, because the letter is dated in April, and it is one year from that date.
I have to inform you that the department will enter into a contract with you for one year for maintaining the buoy service on the Napanee river for the sum of $60 per annum, the amount paid formerly for the service.
If the department had, in pursuance of their evident intention, at the date on which they wrote that letter, sent the contract dated, April, 1903, none of the difficulty would have arisen. But the department having omitted to carry out what they evidently contemplated, has resulted in the river to this hour being unbuoyed, to the danger of craft navigating this narrow and tortuous stream. I know the river and it is quite incorrect to say that because the water is high this year, dangers to navigation do not exist. The dangers, as a matter of fact, are intensified because of that reason. The river has extensive marshes, particularly on one side, and it is more difficult for a vessel to keep in the channel when the water is high, because when the water is, low t;he land marks would be more apparent. The government has therefore made the initial mistake departmentally, in not sending the contract in April when they stated they would and afterwards taking advantage of the contract forwarded in the month of June. The department is to blame for leaving the navigation dangerous by not buoying the river up to the present time.
Who is the contractor for placing the buoys at Alberton, Prince Edward Island ?
I cannot state from memory. I will bring the information to-morrow.
Was the work given by tender, or by private arrangement ?
I am informed that my officials think it was continued from year to year.
Without advertisement?
I am not sure, but that is the information I have.
Who has the contract for placing the buoys at Summerside ?
I will bring down the information later.

I do not think it would be too great flattery to the minister to say that in the course of the evening he has given us one or two small pieces of information. I asked him a question some hours ago which would help us to discover what value we could place on even the little information we got from him. The minister stated on several occasions that he always paid $05 a ton for the carbide, and ir, view of the question asked it was important that his answer should be correct. I called his attention to this fact that according to the Auditor General's Report he had paid at the rate of $100 per ton for carbide. It is important for the House to know how far we can trust to the accuracy of the Auditor General or to the accuracy of the minister's statements.
What was the quantity ?
It was only 400 pounds, but what difference does that make ?
You can make the difference.

It may make very little difference to the minister whether his statement is true or whether it is not, but it does make a lot of difference to the country. Does the minister contend that because it is a small quantity he had to pay $100 a ton ? The minister apparently will not answer. It may be that since he became minister the cerebral end of his corporation occupies more cubic feet than formerly. I submit that a member of this House has the right to know how far the minister's statements can be relied upon. I know from experience that you can buy 400 pounds of carbide at the rate of $65 a ton, because I have repeatedly done it myself. Why should the minister pay more? Perhaps the minister's statement in this respect may throw a side light on the accuracy of his other statements, and if his other statements are not more correct than this, I would like to know why the minister should attempt to give any information to the House at all on this or any other matter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The minister has given no satisfactory reason why the buoys are not placed on the Napanee river. A lot of money was spent by the steamer 'Scout' last year in placing buoys between Montreal and Kingston. She placed a number of buoys opposite Gananoque among the Thousand Islands, on some very dangerous shoals but she failed to pick them up again and now they are scattered all over the
river in places where there are no shoals. Is it the intention of the minister to have them replaced this summer or to have them floating around the river as at present ?

The information of my officials is that these buoys were placed at the demand of the hon. gentle-^ man, at his special request, with the under-1 standing that they would not be picked up by our steamers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The arrangements were made altogether through Mr. Britton, and the department. The hon. gentleman has no right to refer to me in the matter.
That is the information I get.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If you get that information from your department your officers are not worthy of giving you information. The arrangement was made with Mr. Britton. I know all about it, and I know they were placed through Mr. Britton who had been a candidate for the Liberal party there several times and I presume has the confidence of the department and with whom I suppose the department consult. It was he who arranged for having these buoys placed there and he takes all the credit. The department left them there, the ice swept them about and they are floating all around now. The * Scout ' passes there every few days ; why does she not replace them.

The information of my officer is that Mr. Britton may have been present but that the hon. gentleman himself was present, and it was arranged that the buoys would be put out but would not be taken up in the fall by our steamers. I have no other statement to make.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They are there now, government property, floating around the river. The late minister (Mr. Sutherland) went over the river, saw these dangerous shoals, agreed to put buoys there and did put them there. If there was any arrangement made with Mr. Britton or any one else, about taking them up I know nothing about ill., The hon. member for Toronto some time ago, asked the minister on whose representations the change was made from oil to acetylene gas in lighthouses. Was that recommended by Mr. Anderson ?

I have said half a dozen times that the change was made in the regular course of business. I found that the policy of the department through the engineer was perfectly satisfactory. I did not inquire whether Mr. Alexander or Mri Fraser or some one else had recommended it, but I found that it was the policy of the department to replace the oil lamps by acetylene gas wherever necessary.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Was there a report from the engineer ?
X suppose so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Can your officers not inform you ? I am informed that your engineer reported against it.
I am informed that Colonel Anderson himself started the first experiments. I understand the latest improvements on the route were made under Mr. Fraser afterwards.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then it was Mr. Fraser who recommended it to the department ? Somebody must have made a report recommending the change. The opposition are prepared and willing to grant all the money required for the improvement of the lights. I would like to have the minister brifng down the report from his chief engineer or the engineer whoever he was, who made the recommendation that the change should be made. These old and faithful lighthouse keepers after serving the government for many years have been turned out almost on a day's notice.

It has come out that the public service in connection with this department has been neglected, and the minister has given a most remarkably excuse. He has said that no accident has occurred from this neglect. Is that a reasonable or fair excuse to give ? If the same principle is applied to the lower St. Lawrence and the outlet to the ocean, I do not know what the results may be in the future. The excuse is weak, puerile and altogether unbecoming and unworthy of a minister.

I think that the House is entitled to the information as to whose recommendation was received in reference to this change. There is an impression that while the lighting may be an improvement, there may be an increase in the price that would not warrant the change. We should! know at least who recommended the change and whether it was recommended by a competent person.

The experiments were begun by the chief engineer, Col. Anderson, and by Mr. Noble. They were begun before I had charge of the department. The result of the experiments was that the department a couple of years ago decided to put the system in operation. Since then it has been perfected, better apparatus has been secured, and the new system has given every satisfaction. There is no written recommendation or report that I know of, but if the hon. gentleman wants to insinuate that Col Anderson, the chief engineer. was opposed to the change, he is mistaken. A year ago. when there was an excursion to the Montreal harbour, and Mr. PREFONTAINE. '
when the most important men of Montreal interested in shipping were complimenting the department on the improvements made in the lighting, Col. Anderson endorsed everything that had been done.

I made no insinuation regarding Col. Anderson being either in favour or against the change, but I only asked whether there was not a report recommending it. The minister says that the experiment was begun before he had charge of thy department, but the records of the department are at his disposal, and if there be any recommendation either one way or the other, he ought to be able to procure it.

I would ask my hon. friend as a business man, what difference would it make, if the change be a good one, whether it was recommended by Peter, John or Tom. The result is perfectly satisfactory not only to the department but to every body interested in shipping, and I do not see what more any one else can want.

All I want to get at is whether the department undertook to change the lighting without having the report of some one recommending the change. I cannot imagine any business man changing a whole system of lighting without having had an inquiry made by some one competent to judge and obtaining the report of that person. Will the minister give us the assurance that he will endeavour to ascertain whether there is any such report or recommendation, and if so submit it to the House ?

The minister is only wasting his own time and mat of the committee in putting up a man of straw only to knock him down. I did not object to the improvements. They may be all right, so far as I know. He says that there were no written reports, but that there may have been verbal ones. I take it that he did not order these changes without consulting some one and without having some one advise him that this would be a wise expenditure. All I asked was that, if there were any written reports, the hon. minister should bring them down. The hon. gentleman spoke of the upper lakes, but when he came to speak of improvements made there he mentioned one at Gananoque. He does not seem to use the expression ' upper lakes ' in the same way I have been accustomed to hear it used. We speak of the upper lakes as the waters from Georgian Bay upwards. Is any provision to be made for these waters ?
Not under this vote. But, under a supplementary vote wo are asking enough money to provide a depot on Georgian Bay so as to provide the aids to navigation as fast as possible.
When the hon. minister speaks of a depot, does he mean a manufacturing establishment to turn out these gas buoys ?

No, we do not manufacture the gas buoys. We have been trying to get them in Canada. Since I have been at the head of the department I have approached all the manufacturers in Montreal and Toronto and tried to convince them of the advantage they would gain by manufacturing these buoys. They are made of steel plates welded together, and the manufacture of them is very costly. There is no plant for that purpose now in Canada, and we have been obliged to import them from Germany. They are not made in the United States either, for that country has to import them* from Germany also. I understand that Mr. Poison has stated that if there was sufficient market for them, and if the department would purchase them in sufficient quantity, he would install the necessary machinery. The machinery for manufacturing these buoys, according to the information I have obtained from Mr. Poison as well as from the Laurie works in Montreal, would cost about $100,000. It stands to reason that the principal purchaser would be the government. The work that is done at Prescott consists in the preparation of the gas, the manufacture of lanterns ancf other apparatus required. The depot is there, also the headquarters of the



buoy service between Montreal and Kingston. Formerly such an expensive plant was not required, because there were not so many buoys and lights and signals in use. The department is now in a better position to give the necessary service which is required. The matter is not new, it came before the House last year. We have discussed the question with business men in-i terested in navigation between Montreal and the lakes.

I would like to point out that when we have tried to get some statement from the hon. minister as to who recommended the acetylene gas he replied that he did not know if there were any written reports. Now it is not to be expected that every member of this House can read all the reports laid before us from time to time. If the hon. gentleman had applied to; his deputy, he could have ascertained the page and he could have referred us to page 94 of his own report, appendix No. 5, which tells us that Mr. Fraser dealt extensively with acetylene gas lights. If the minister had given us this information promptly less time would have been taken up.
Mr, SPROULE, What do these tanks cost each, I mean one that runs six months or a year ?

About $875. In answer to the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), I may say that the report of Mr. J. F. Fraser was dated on the 31st of December, 1903. But I do not know that Mr. Fraser had anything to do with it. Besides Mr. J. F. Fraser there is another Mr. Fraser, who is assistant to Col. Anderson himself. So it is not extraordinary that Mr. J. F. Fraser in his report as commissioner of lights should have treated, this question. He should not be reproached for it, nor should the government.
Mr* INGRAM. The minister might have told us that we could find the report in ap-j pendix 5, page 19 of his report.

The question put by the hon. member was whether, before beginning the experiment of the acetylene system, there was a report. As I explained, that was before I took charge of the department. The report to which the hon. gentleman makes allusion is that of Mr. ,T. F. Fraser, and is dated 31st December, 1903. The experiments had been made previously to that, and it was therefore no longer an experiment.

There is no absolute recommendation in this report that these are the proper lights to adopt, it merely deals with the experiments that have been made. If the hon. gentleman wants to expedite business, let him tell us where we can get this information. We have not got time to go through all these blue-books. We expect
the minister and his officers to point out to us where the information is to be found, because they are familiar with their own reports.

The report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries was laid on the table of the House at the beginning of the session. Now does the hon. gentleman suppose that my officers, even those who prepared the reports and appendices, are in a position to tell me the precise page where I can find any particulars ?
Certainly.

It is impossible, no man's brains are equal to the task. It is not reasonable to ask the officials to do this for the members. The report is laid before the House on purpose to inform the members of its contents, and if the members of the House are not intelligent enough to read the report and post themselves, they have no right to blame the minister or his officials because they are not ready to point out the precise page where you will find such and such a thing.

I will guarantee that the hon. gentlemen will not get any of his brother ministers in the cabinet to endorse him in that statement. Does the hon. gentleman pretend to say that the Auditor General's Report, that contains hundreds of pages, along with the hon. gentleman's own two departmental reports, also many others of great size, are such that the members of the House can master all the details contained in them ? We have not the time to peruse all the blue-books that are laid on the table of the House and attend to our other duties besides. It is simply impossible and I can tell my hon. friend that if I confined myself to the mastering of the details of these two blue-bodks since the opening of the session to now I could tell him the page in which to find this information. Here is the hon. minister and his officers handling this department from January to December, and yet they tell us they cannot point out in the appendix to these two blue-books where we can find this information ?

Why did you not
ask me ?
We have been asking you all along.

I must deny that. If you had asked me where you could find this information from my reports I would have given you an answer at once. But, when you ask me that question in regard to all the reports in my department it is a different ching. You want me to look in all the pigeon holes of my department for reports, imaginary and otherwise. If the hon. gentleman had asked where this

subject was treated In the report of the department 1 would have looked it up and given him the information.
My hon. friend from East Grey simply asked whether there were any reports, and the minister said he did not know whether there were any or not.

That was not the
report asked for.
That was the report. The report asked for was in regard to these experiments which were carried out with the steamer ' Scout.'

['I expected that we would have been able to conclude this debate to-night ; but in view of the great importance which the subject has attained in the country, I think every latitude should be given to the other side to ventilate their grievances, and therefore I assent to the motion.']
FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think that any one in the House or in the country will deny the importance of the incident to which I propose to direct; attention this afternoon and with respect to which I propose to move a resolution irf amendment to that which has been proposed by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I regret that I was not able to give to the House last evening the tenor of this resolution, but I have sent a copy of it to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) at the earliest possible moment this morning, after it had been completed. The incident to which I refer touches vitally the question whether or not we are to have in Canada a non-partisan militia force, or whether we are to have in this country partisan politics introduced into the appointment of officers and the recommendations of men for commissions in that force. I would not suppose that there could be any two opinions on what should be the correct course. Up to the present time we have not beard a great deal of politics being introduced at least into this portion of the administration of the department. I do not remember in my own province ever hearing a man's political opinions discussed in connection with an appointment to a position in the militia. It would be extremely regrettable if partisan political considerations should be allowed to interpose between the General Officer Commanding and those officers who are subordinate to him. To permit, that is to permit interference by politicians with men who are engaged in the performance of their duty, and to interfere with an officer in the performance of his duty, in that regard is certain to result in the most disastrous effect upon the militia force of this country.
The incident with which we are especially concerned this afternoon, is that which relates to the organization of the 13th Scottish Light Dragoons, in the eastern townships of the province of Quebec. The circumstances connected with the case have been placed quite fully before the House and the country. I shall have to come to a consideration of the. correspondence which has been brought down before I conclude my remarks, but let me say for the present that having read everything that

has been published on the subject, having carefully examined the correspondence which has been brought down, having listened to the statements made in this House by the hon. the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) and the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher)' I cannot find one jot or tittle of evidence which indicates that Colonel Smart or Colonel Whitley, his brigadier, were influenced by any political considerations whatever, in the establishment of that regiment until the Minister of Agriculture imposed such considerations upon them. I think the evidence is absolutely conclusive that these gentlemen were simply endeavouring to find the best available men, to obtain qualified men when they could obtain qualified men and in the absence of men who were *qualified, that their efforts were solely and absolutely directed to appointing the most efficient men in order that that regiment might be put on the most efficient possible basis. Mere motives of self-interest would lead these men to adopt that course. Why should Colonel Smart, a man responsible for that regiment, a man only desirous to put it on the best possible basis, seek to introduce political considerations ? Colonel Smart is not a partisan ; I do not know what his politics are, I do not know whether he has any pronounced legal opinions. Certainly he is not a Conservative partisan and I do not think he is a Liberal partisapj Colonel Whitley is, I understand, a Liberal in politics. I have never heard that he is a political partisan but I understand that his political sympathies are with the party in power. Therefore there is no possible reason to suppose that either one of these men would have been influenced by any political considerations, certainly not by any political considerations that would lend either one of them to favour the Conservative party in the making of appointments.
The question is whether or not partisan politics were introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) into the organization of that regiment. We have had; upon that subject a statement in this House by the hon. gentleman himself, and also a statement by the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) and I propose to call attention in the first place to what the Minister of Agriculture himself has said upon the subject in order that I may in that way lead up to some consideration of the correspondence which has been brought down. The statement of the Minister of Agriculture is to be found in ' Hansard ' at page 4581. I shall not read the whole of it, hon. gentlemen are familiar with it. It is to this effect :
In regard to Lord Dundonald's general statement that I interfered with the organization of the corps, and with the names of the other proposed officers of the corps as well as Dr. Pickel's, let me say this r That the only

grounds on which I made any suggestions in regard to the establishment of this corps were the immense importance of the appointment of leading officers with military qualifications, who knew the country and the people of the eastern townships, the district where the corps was to be established.
Now, it we were to stop there end take that statement of the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) supported as it was by the hon. the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) we might only regard the interference of the Minister of Agriculture as meddlesome, and we need not regard it as absolutely vicious. He would be only meddling in that which other men were much better qualified to do. If his interference had stopped there and had been directed solely to that object, the criticism which I am about to make this afternoon would not have been so well deserved although I do not see any reason why the Minister of Agriculture should interpose his wonderful military knowledge, between the General Officer Commanding and those men who, under the General Officer, were charged with the duty of organizing this regiment. I would not suppose that, apart from political considerations, the Minister of Agriculture would feel himself qualified to over-ride the opinions of these gentlemen so far as military qualifications are concerned, because it is in regard to military qualifications that he is speaking in the portion of his remarks to which I have called attention.	,
Having thus called the Minister of Agriculture as a witness in his own behalf and having quoted that portion of the written) statement which he made before this House, let us now see what he said further on the subject, after a memorandum from Lord Dundonald had been read, and let us see whether or not the statement which I have just read emanating from his own lips is supported by his own language on the very same day, in fact only a few minutes afterwards. On page 4005 he said this :
I found this list of proposed names for the staff for the neighbourhood of Sweetsburg. First, Mr. John M. Gibson, a nephew of Senator Baker, and talked of as a possible Conservative candidate, in the constituency of Mis-sisquoi to be third in command of that regiment.
If my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture was concerning himself alone with the military qualifications of the gentlemen who were proposed to be recommended for that regiment, why was it necessary for him to inquire or to state the political opinions or the relationship of this gentleman, to whom I have just referred. He proceeded then as follows :
Dr. Pickel, one of the strongest Conservative workers of the neighbourhood, and a family connection of Senator Baker, to be major in command of the squadron which, though gazetted
for Adamsville, was to be changed to Sweetsburg to suit his convenience.
Do we find any reference there to the military qualifications of this gentleman ? No, we find there simply a reference to his political opinions and to his relationship to this same Senator Baker who seems to be the bete noir of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, and who has influenced unconsciously the hon. Minister of Agriculture in regard to this important matter hy the mere fact of his having opposed him, as he had a perfect right to do, in his political campaigns in the eastern townships. But, surely we do not find in these words of the lion. Minister of Agriculture any question of the military qualifications of Dr. Pickel. The minister is interested merely in his political opinions and his relationship to this same Senator Baker. What is the next remark ? It is this :

Baker, sou of Senator Baker, to be senior captain of the said squadron.
No objection to the military qualifications of Captain Baker but merely a statement that ne happens, unfortunately, to be related to Senator Baker-unfortunately according to the view of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, because if Captain Baker had not been the son of his father there would have been no objection to him by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture. Then, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture proceeds as follows :

Pickel, son-in-law of Senator Baker, to be the junior captain of the said squadron.
The hon. Minister of Agriculture is unable to get Senator Baker out of his mind. Senator Baker looms up before him in connection with every one of these gentlemen, and it is not their military qualifications but their connection with Senator Baker which so thoroughly alarms him in connection with the appointments to his regiment. He proceeds :
Then there were the names of two gentlemen, Messrs. Steaoie and Reynolds, of Montreal, to be lieutenants. And down at the bottom of the list Mr. Thos. F. Cotton, a Liberal, son-in-law of the above-mentioned John M. Gibson, and grand nephew of Senator Baker.
It reminds one of a genealogical table.
Hear, hear.

My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) smiles I am speaking of the remarks of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. This hon. gentleman who first told us that he was considering merely the qualifications of these officers has not one word to say about their military qualifications in what I have read, but lie concerns himself solely with their relationship to Senator Baker and with their

political opinions.. Yet lie bad the audacity to stand up in this House and say that his interference in the affairs of that regiment was concerned solely and absolutely-^ with the military qualifications of tli officers. He may be able to reconcile those statements. I am not able to reconcile them. I regard one statement as absolutely inconsistent with the other statement. But, X will go further and quote again from what the hon. gentleman said :

And I said that, if such a recommendation as that were to go through and be known in the district of Bedford, nothing under heaven would remove the impression from the people of the county and of the country that the new regiment was to be conducted on the lines of the old regiments there, and that it would receive its bap-Mr. R. The only grounds on which I made any suggestion in regard to the establishment of this corps, were the immense importance of the appointment of leading officers with military qualifications.
In the minister's own speech delivered a few minutes afterwards, and in the very Order in Council which seeks to justify him. there is a confession of his interference on political grounds. Hughes). Lord Dundonald says.
Shortly after the promulgation of the order authorizing the organization of the regiment, I received an order from Sir Frederick Borden to Colonel Pinault, the Deputy Minister of Militia, desiring him to stop the organization.
We have never yet had any explanation in this House as to how the Minister of Militia was induced to issue that order, stopping the organization of the regiment. Although it is said these reasons were communicated to the General Officer Commanding, they have not been communicated to this House, and knowing what we do of the conduct of the hon. minister afterwards, we cannot fail to come to the conclusion that it was the indirect interposition of the Minister of Agriculture which induced the Minister of Militia to make that order, and that it was for these partisan purposes which are disclosed in the correspondence, that the order was issued stopping and delaying the organization of that regiment. Lord Dundonald continues.
No explanation or reason for this step was vouchsafed, but indirectly I learned that the Minister of Agriculture was responsible for the delay which thus occurred.
And yet, this is the minister who, in his first statement at least to this House, declared that his interference was for no other reason than to secure the appointment of properly qualified officers. Colonel Smart continues :
This I refused to do, as I had invited Dr. Pickel to come into the regiment, and told Mr. Fisher- that some one else would have to he responsible for the withdrawal of Dr. Pickel s name.

1 had submitted Mr. Pickel's name, recommending that he be appointed captain in ' E Squadron, but Mr. Fisher insisted that I substitute the name of Lieutenant R. Steacie, making him captain and Mr. Pickel first lieutenant.
I pointed out to Mr. Fisher that Mr. Pickel, being a resident of the townships, was entitled to a senior rank in preference to Mr. Steacie, who lives in Montreal, and, moreover, as Mr. Steacie is a relative of mine, it would place me in a false position, and appear as though I was unduly advancing him at the expense of others. However, Mr. Fisher evidently _ had his mind made up on the matter and insisted on the change, to which 1 reluctantly agreed. I regret to say that this caused some dissatisfaction, and I would like at the first opportunity to transfer Mr. Steacie to another squadron and recommend Mr. Pickel for his captaincy.
And let us see what the Minister of Agriculture bad to do with the case of Captain Converse, a gentleman who in the memorandum brought down only yesterday by the government, is described as the most capable cavalry officer in Canada. Colonel Smart says :
There has been no contradiction in this House, of that statement up to the present. But that is not the chief part of the indictment against the Minister of Agriculture. because we have the direct and hitherto uncontradicted statement of the officer commanding this regiment, and whose duty it was to organize the regiment, as to the part which the Minister of Agriculture took in this matter. Colonel Smart says in his letter to Lord Dundonald :
I submitted the name of Dr. F. H. Pickel, who is mayor of the town of Sweetsburg, and warden of the county of Missisquoi, to he major in command of ' E ' Squadron. Dr Pickel is a gentleman of means, can ride fairly well, and was quite willing to take the necessary time to qualify himself for the position of major. Mr. Fisher objected to him for no other reason than that he was a strong political opponent of his and was quite determined to block the whole organization, unless Dr. Pickel's name was withdrawn.
With -regard to the' adjutancy, Captain Converse, whom I selected for this position, has served in the militia for about (15) fifteen years and for a long time served as sergeant-major in the Duke of York's Hussars. Mr. Fisher asked me to drop this gentleman and substitute Mr. Adams, of the 6th Hussars, a gentleman who is very deaf, and whom I -consider physically unfit for the position.
But, you will observe- throughout all, that the Minister of Agriculture is solely concerned with obtaining officers qualified for the position, and for that reason he wanted to put to one side Captain Converse who is described as the best cavalry officer in Canada, and to substitute for him Mr. Adams, a gentleman so deaf as to be incapable of acting, in the opinion of Colonel Smart. And, according to the statement of Colonel Smart, Captain Adams was so sure of the effect which political power in the hands of the minister could exercise,

that he openly threatened Colonel Smart in the presence of Colonel Whitley with the exercise of his political influence. And, Sir, the political influence which Mr. Adams declared he could have exercised, has been very effectively exercised by the Minister of Agriculture. I venture to say, that if the government sees fit to grant an inquiry into that most important statement made by Colonel Smart as to the threats of Captain Adams, they will find that Colonel Smart is corroborated by Colonel Whitley, his brigadier. Colonel Smart says :
I absolutely declined to consider this at all, and Mr. Fisher waived his objections.
But he was not finished with Mr. Adams yet, as we shall see.
He then asked me to recommend Mr. Adams for major to command ' E ' squadron, and this I flatly declined to do.
Mr. Fisher asked Colonel Smart to recommend Mr. Adams in place of Dr. Pickel whom Mr. Fisher had rejected, and yet this is the hon. gentleman who was concerned solely with assisting the Colonel who was to organize the regiment, in the selection of officers duly qualified for command. The Minister of Agriculture seems to have regarded his own judgment as absolutely superior to that of these experienced officers; he thought himself much more competent and more qualified to select officers, having regard to military qualifications, than were the experienced military men whom this country paid to discharge that duty.
Now, Sir, I shall consider for a moment what is the position of the General Officer Commanding, and what is the position of the Minister himself ? This regiment was about to be organized and the commanding officer had been chosen, whose duty was to select and report the names of his subordinate officers for recommendation by the General Officer Commanding. . After the General Officer Commanding had recommended these names to the Minister of Militia, the Minister of Militia would of course have the responsibility of either approving of them or rejecting them. There is no question of that, under the system of government which we have in this country. Let us see what the statute says about the status of the Minister of Militia :
There shall be a Minister of Militia and Defence^ who shall be charged with and be responsible for the administration of militia affairs including all matters involving (expenditure and of the fortifications, gun-boats ordnance, ammunition, arms, armouries, stores, munitions and habiliments of war belonging to Canada.

Has Colonel Whitley made that request by letter or orally ?
By telephone, to-day.

Well, I do not know why the letters of a brigadier in the militia to the Minister of Agriculture should be marked private. The Minister of Agriculture has some status in this matter or he has no status. I think he has no status. If he claims to have a status which justifies him in interfering with the affairs of this regiment, why is it that official communications respecting the organization of this regiment from an officer of Canada to the Minister of Agriculture should be marked private, and that this House should be deprived of them because either the Minister of Agriculture or Colonel Whitley thinks they should not be brought down ?
Why may we not have all communications in the Department of Militia or any other public department marked private ? Why may we not have every report by a paid officer of this country marked private, and have ministers of the Crown refuse to have them brought down because they are marked private ? Where are we to stop ? Do not those letters relate to the organization of this regiment ? Will my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture deny that ? And yet these letters are to be withheld from parliament because Colonel Whitley/ an officer paid by this country for his services, thinks they should not be brought down.
I do not know whether any suggestion was made to Colonel "Whitley on that point; I do not know whether any intimation was given to him. From what I have heard of that gallant gentleman, I would not believe that he would write letters which he was not willing to have placed before parliament and the country unless he was led into some specious intrigue by the Minister of Agriculture which he might not be willing to disclose. Apart from that, I do not know of any reason why letters of Colonel Whitley or letters of any other officer of the militia with regard to matters of this kind should not be laid before this House. There were inclosures in one of these letters of Colonel Whitley. They are referred to on page 26 of this memorandum. The Minister of Agriculture says this, in his letter dated May 20, 1904 :
I have read your letters and the inclosures, and want to assure you not only that I am very glad things have now been tfettled, but that I appreciate the efforts which you and Colonel Smart have made to make things satisfactory.
Are the inclosures confidential ? Might I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture whether the inclosures were -also confidential ?
They are sent back to Colonel Whitley at his request. They are not in my possession. I do not know anything about them beyond having looked them over.

Colonel Whitley is I believe, the brigadier of the eastern townships and a salaried officer of this government. If he has documents of that kind in his possession, they can be produced. The government can produce them, if they desire, but we cannot. Why were not these inclosures brought down ? But that is not all. The Minister of Agriculture proceeds as follows
I have written to our friends telling them that this has been done and urging them to take hold of their work energetically and loyally, and I am sure they will do so.
Why should not these' letters to ' our friends' be produced? They would show to what extent the Minister of Agriculture was interfering in the affairs of the regiment.

I take it for granted he lias written nothing of which he is ashamed. If he is not ashamed of them, why does he not bring these letters down ? If he was interfering in the organization of this regiment, he must have been doing so as a public man, as one having some official status ; and as he wrote to *Colonel Whitley and in that letter referred to inclosures, and as his own letter has been brought down, why should not the documents mentioned in that letter be also brought down ? How it is that these docu: ments are any more private or privileged than the letter itself ? That letter could just as well be regarded as private as the documents referred to in it. Yet we have not one of these various documents to which I have referred. For some reason that 1 cannot very well appreciate, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture thinks they should not be produced.
As I have said already, the interference of my hon. friend in this matter evidently began early in March and was exercised up to the 20th of May, when lie said he was acting as Minister of Militia. I think the Minister of Militia and Defence owes it to himself, to rise in this debate and explain to the House, in the first place, why it was he saw fit in April to stop the organization of this regiment which he himself had directed in February, and why, in the next place he supplemented that direction by the imperative command contained in the order of April 29th which I have just read. Was it, by any chance, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture ? And was there any question of introducing politics in it ?
